title: Book Ten opens: was the account of the tent enough?
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK TEN. Still on the same subjects, and on the things in the holy tent.
Cyril: Palladius, has the account we gave of the holy tent and of the things in it been clear to you, and enough?
translator_notes: The opening question has no speaker siglum in PG; it is Cyril's, since he addresses Palladius, so the label 'Cyril:' is supplied. σκηνή of Moses is rendered 'tent' throughout Book 10, as in Books 3 and 9. No Scripture.

title: Why Moses, not Joshua, set up the tent
english: Palladius: Very clear indeed, but far from enough.

Cyril: Then would you like us to go back with all eagerness to the point that seems to have been left out of what we said about it? For you think, I suppose, and naturally so, that we must add an account that makes clear how it was set up for us, and when and how the ordinances and laws connected with it were established, together with its dedication, its sanctification and its judgment.
Palladius: Then explain each of these in turn, for you are thinking rightly.

Cyril: I will speak, then. But you in turn must be indulgent, bearing in mind how altogether difficult these contemplations are. If at any point I happen to say something that misses precision and strays from what ought to be said, reshape it and set it right; for I will make you a partner and helper in my words.
Palladius: Go on, trusting in God.

Cyril: When the work on the holy tent had been fully completed, and each of the things in it had been made with wisdom and skill after the beauty shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘On one day of the first month, at the new moon, you shall set up the tent of witness’ (Exodus 40:2). And again, further on: ‘And it came to pass,’ it says, ‘in the first month, in the second year after they went out of Egypt, at the new moon, that the tent was set up, and Moses set up the tent’ (Exodus 40:17–18). So the ancient tent was set up as God willed. It was the tent of the Church that is understood in Christ, and it showed beforehand in itself, very clearly, the types of that Church. Let us inquire closely, if you agree, why it was set up by Moses rather than by another, while Joshua the son of Nun is passed over in silence for the present. Yet Joshua always stood beside the most excellent Moses (Exodus 24:13); he went up with him onto Mount Sinai, and he made war and marched out against Amalek at Moses’ word. For Moses said to him: ‘Choose for yourself mighty men, and go out and draw up for battle against Amalek tomorrow’ (Exodus 17:9). And he drew up for battle, and he won (Exodus 17:10–13). What, then, is the reason for this? Is it not worth examining?
Palladius: Certainly it is.

Cyril: If anyone chooses to work out, as exactly as he can, the meaning of the mystery in each of these events, he will say in amazement: ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!’ (Romans 11:33). See how subtle and how necessary the sense of each detail is. When the inspired Moses goes up the mountain, Joshua goes up with him; for the Father cannot be approached in any other way than through the Son. Indeed, the saying is true: ‘No one comes to the Father except through me’ (John 14:6). So even for the saints themselves the approach is in Christ. No one could spring up, as onto a mountain, to some lofty and surpassing contemplation; nor, I think, could anyone come near to God — by way of
translator_notes: Exodus 40:2 LXX reads 'Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ μιᾷ' (a Hebraism for 'on the first day'); rendered 'On one day' because Cyril's exegesis in §§3-4 turns on 'one day'. Exodus 40:17-18: Cyril's quotation runs from verse 17 into the first clause of verse 18. 'The beauty shown on the mountain' alludes to Exodus 25:40 (LXX 'τὸν τύπον τὸν δεδειγμένον σοι ἐν τῷ ὄρει'); cf. Exodus 25:9. 'Always stood beside' echoes Exodus 24:13 LXX 'Ἰησοῦς ὁ παρεστηκὼς αὐτῷ', which also records Joshua going up the mountain with Moses. Exodus 17:9 LXX has 'Ἐπίλεξον'; Cyril's 'Ἐπίλεξαι' is a middle form, same sense. Joshua is 'Ἰησοῦς' in Greek, the same name as Jesus; Cyril's typology (Joshua goes up with Moses as the Son leads to the Father) depends on this, but the English follows Book 3 and says 'Joshua'. 'δικαιώματα' may echo Hebrews 9:1 ('δικαιώματα λατρείας'); not cited. 'κρίσις' (judgment) left plain; it may point to the 'oracle of judgment' (Exodus 28:15, 28:30), not cited. The section ends mid-word (συν|αφείας); the English breaks at 'by way of' and resumes in §3 with 'union'.

title: Christ makes the way to God passable; the law builds the Church
english: union, I mean, in the life lived in the Spirit and in holiness — unless Emmanuel were with him, making what is beyond human reach passable on foot and even on horseback. And this, I think, is what was spoken through the voice of Isaiah: ‘Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and all the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough places smooth roads’ (Isaiah 40:4; Luke 3:5). For in Christ even the steep places are smooth for us, and rough ground can be walked; the hard roads lie clear and level. Indeed, as the prophet himself says again elsewhere: ‘The way of the godly has become straight, and the way of the godly is made ready’ (Isaiah 26:7). So of necessity Joshua goes up with the inspired Moses. For, as I said, the Father is approached through the Son, and he is the Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), who joins us through himself and carries us up to heights beyond nature. Joshua drew up for battle with picked men and defeated Amalek. For Christ chose the saints, whose firstfruits were the inspired disciples, and conquered the ruler of this age. But Moses was the one who gave the command; for the Son came under the law (Galatians 4:4), though as God he is the Lawgiver. And the battle was not fought on the very day on which Moses spoke, but on the next day, that is, it was put off to a later time. For the law foretold what was to come, and, if it is understood spiritually, it contains a splendid account of the Savior’s mighty deeds. This, I think, is also why it was Moses who set up the holy tent. For the training given through the law has its part in the forming of the Church. It leads us as a tutor to Christ (Galatians 3:24), who is the head of the Church (Ephesians 5:23; Colossians 1:18) and its whole structure, ‘the pillar and foundation of the truth,’ as it is written (1 Timothy 3:15). Indeed Christ said to the Jews: ‘If you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote about me’ (John 5:46). So Moses too, that is, the training given through the law, builds the Church of Christ, showing beforehand, as though still in shadows, the mystery concerning it. The person of Moses sometimes stands for the law given through him, as is rightly said in the parables of the Gospel: ‘They have Moses and the prophets’ (Luke 16:29).
Palladius: You have spoken rightly.

Cyril: And what, in turn, might it mean that the holy tent had to be pitched on one day, at the new moon of the first month, and in the second year? Come, let us explain it, tracking down the truth and what future readers will judge best. The one day points to the saving time for which we prayed so long, in which the Only-begotten became man and by the death of his own flesh won those on earth for God the Father. And this time is one for all. For having died once, he dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him, as the Scriptures say (Romans 6:9–10). For we shall no longer expect the Son to die for us and for the spirits in Hades, nor yet
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence (PG column break inside συναφείας); the paragraph continues Cyril's turn from §2, so it carries no speaker label (as in Book 3 continuation rows). 'In spirit' (ἐν πνεύματι) taken as the Holy Spirit and capitalised; it could mean 'spiritual'. The Isaiah quotation: Cyril names Isaiah 40:4, but his last clause ('αἱ τραχεῖαι εἰς ὁδοὺς λείας') follows Luke 3:5, not LXX Isaiah ('ἡ τραχεῖα εἰς πεδία'); both cited. Isaiah 26:7 matches LXX exactly. 'The Mediator' cites 1 Timothy 2:5 as a clear allusion. 'The ruler of this age' (ἀρχηγὸν τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου) may echo John 12:31 or 2 Corinthians 4:4; doubtful, not cited. 'Came under the law' = Galatians 4:4 'γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον'. 'Leads us as a tutor to Christ' = Galatians 3:24. Head of the Church: Colossians 1:18 (cf. Ephesians 5:23). 1 Timothy 3:15 calls the Church 'pillar and foundation of the truth'; Cyril's grammar here applies the phrase to Christ, who is the Church's whole frame; kept as he has it. 'As though still in shadows' may echo Hebrews 10:1; not cited. Romans 6:9 is paraphrased with 6:10 ('ἐφάπαξ'); Cyril's future 'κυριεύσει' differs from NT 'κυριεύει'. 'The spirits in Hades' may echo 1 Peter 3:19; not cited. 'Won those on earth for God' may echo Revelation 5:9; not cited. Ends mid-sentence ('ἀλλ' οὐδὲ'); resumes in §4.

title: One day of salvation; the Church built in believers
english: that there will be a second firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). For if there is to be no more death, how could there be a resurrection? So we may say without falsehood that this time is one, as I said just now, and the day is one. The prophet too mentioned this day, speaking as in the person of God: ‘In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you’ (Isaiah 49:8). And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation’ (2 Corinthians 6:2). On that day Christ came back to life from the dead, having destroyed the grim power of death; and then he also appointed the holy apostles as builders, so to speak, and spiritual craftsmen of the Church from the Gentiles, saying: ‘Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age’ (Matthew 28:19–20). Or would you not say that this is what forms the Church?
Palladius: What exactly do you mean?

Cyril: The faith handed down through the holy teachers of the mysteries, and the way of life that has been proclaimed, I mean the life in Christ, and the union with God through holy baptism, by sharing in the Holy Spirit. For so Paul addressed us, saying: ‘And you, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5), into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit’ (Ephesians 2:21–22). For of old Christ was foreshadowed in the holy tent as though in various vessels: as the golden censer, as the ark, as the lampstand, and also as the table and what was set on it. But now, in the present time, each of those who have believed is, I think, called a house and temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16), since he has Christ dwelling within him. For Christ dwells in our hearts through faith, as it is written (Ephesians 3:17). He is by nature one and the same, even when he is thought of together with the flesh; for there is ‘one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things’ (1 Corinthians 8:6). Yet through the various properties of his Godhead he has in himself, as it were, many forms, and he is understood in various ways. For he is in us as the Word of God, and as wisdom, and light, and life, and the living bread that came from heaven (John 6:51).
Palladius: I understand what you mean.

Cyril: So the time when he became man for us, and the much longed-for day of the resurrection from the dead, were prefigured of old when God said: ‘On one day you shall set up the tent’ (Exodus 40:2). And as for the words ‘and at the new moon of the first month,’ one can see, Palladius, that they were added usefully and of necessity. For as the beginning of a month is the first of its days, that is, the new moon, so the time of his coming among us is a kind of beginning of a new age and the first onset of new times. For ‘in Christ there is a new creation; the old things have passed away’ (2 Corinthians 5:17). And the age that follows this one dawns upon us, as it were, now still seen as in hope, but then to be present
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing Cyril's turn from §3, so no speaker label. 'Firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' = 1 Corinthians 15:20. Isaiah 49:8 matches LXX; 2 Corinthians 6:2 matches the NT. Matthew 28:19-20 quoted nearly verbatim; 'all the days' rendered 'always'. 'The grim power of death' (τὸ ἀμειδὲς τοῦ θανάτου κράτος) may echo Hebrews 2:14; not cited. Cyril attributes the 'living stones' text to Paul, but it joins 1 Peter 2:5 ('ὡς λίθοι ζῶντες οἰκοδομεῖσθε οἶκος πνευματικὸς') with Ephesians 2:21-22 ('εἰς ναὸν ἅγιον ... εἰς κατοικητήριον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πνεύματι'); the attribution is kept as written and both are cited. The list of tent furnishings (golden censer, ark, lampstand, table) resembles Hebrews 9:2-4; not cited. 'And what was set on it': αὐτῇ is feminine and could refer to the table or to the tent; taken as the table (the bread of the Presence, as in Hebrews 9:2). 'House and temple of God' cited to 1 Corinthians 3:16 as a clear allusion. 'Dwells in our hearts through faith' = Ephesians 3:17 (Cyril says 'as it is written'); the subject 'Christ' is repeated in English for clarity, as the Greek subject is the Christ just named. 'One and the same by nature, even when thought of with the flesh' keeps Cyril's Christological terms (κατὰ φύσιν; μετὰ σαρκός). The titles Word, wisdom, light, life are not cited (general titles); only the 'living bread from heaven' is cited, John 6:51. 'The time when he became man' renders ἐνανθρώπησις. 2 Corinthians 5:17: Cyril gives a shortened form ('καινὴ κτίσις ἐν Χριστῷ'), translated as he has it without the verse's 'if anyone is' frame. Ends mid-sentence (παρεσόμενος | ἀληθῶς); §5 resumes with 'in truth'.

title: Spring, the second year, and the Church of the Gentiles; the tent that will not be shaken
english: Cyril: …in truth, when Christ shines on us again with the holy angels in the glory of the Father (Mark 8:38). Then he will take with him those who have chosen to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4) and who have grown rich, through patience, in the surpassing beauty of the Gospel way of life, and he will bring them into the glory and the kingdom long awaited. That those who are in Christ are a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and, as it were, a new budding of times and of things, the figure of the first month (Exodus 40:2) would show this very well. In that month tender grass, freshly sprung, appears on the earth, plants flower again, and the varied beauty of the meadow flowers comes into view, while the fragrance of spring smiles. For it was in such a season, as it were, that Christ called the Church from the Gentiles, saying: ‘Arise, come, my companion, my fair one, my dove; for behold, the winter is past, the rain is gone, it has gone its way; the flowers have appeared in the land; the time of pruning has come’ (Song of Songs 2:10–12). For human nature flourished once more, like a plant, after it had withered away in death because of the transgression in Adam and the sin that tyrannized over us all. And I hear Christ saying through one of the holy prophets as well: ‘I who speak am here, like springtime upon the mountains’ (Isaiah 52:6–7). For what spring does on the mountains and in the woods, crowning the plants with new growth, the coming of our Savior has also brought to completion in us. It came at its appointed time, as in the second year (Exodus 40:17), and not in the first period, when the law was in force together with the choir of the prophets, and when death held sway. For death reigned from Adam until Moses (Romans 5:14). So it was as in the second year, that is, in the time that followed the first, the time of the law, that the Church from the Gentiles shone out, with Christ, the end of the prophets and of the law (Romans 10:4), vividly present to her. Does it seem to you that our argument is speeding toward what is right and true?
Palladius: Entirely so.

Cyril: For my part, I think that the truer tent was announced to us beforehand through the voice of Isaiah, who says, as if to each of those called through faith to righteousness: ‘Your eyes will see Jerusalem, rich cities, tents that will not be shaken; the pegs of its tent will not be moved, and its cords will never be broken, for all time’ (Isaiah 33:20). For the Church is the city of God, which the inspired David also spoke of when he said: ‘Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God’ (Psalm 87:3). For she is rich, made splendid with gifts from above and from heaven, and her foundation and her permanence stand firm and cannot be broken. For ‘the gates of Hades will not prevail against her,’ as the Savior said (Matthew 16:18).
Palladius: Your thinking is entirely right and reasonable.
Cyril: Once the tent had been set up, God, the Master of all, teaches that the things in it had to be placed in order, and not heaped together carelessly, when he says:
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, continuing §4 (‘now seen as in hopes, but then present’ + ἀληθῶς); rendered ‘…in truth, when Christ shines…’ so it joins whatever §4 ends with. ‘With the holy angels in the glory of the Father’ matches Mark 8:38 (also Luke 9:26; Matthew 16:27 has ‘his angels’); Cyril says ‘shines upon’ rather than ‘comes’. ‘First month’ points back to Exodus 40:2 (LXX: on the first day of the first month, at the new moon, set up the tent), expounded in §4; ‘second year’ is Exodus 40:17 LXX (first month of the second year after leaving Egypt). Song of Songs 2:10–12 follows the LXX: καιρὸς τῆς τομῆς = ‘time of pruning’ (Hebrew: time of singing); Cyril’s ἐπορεύθη ἐν αὐτῷ for LXX ἑαυτῷ rendered ‘it has gone its way’. Isaiah 52:6–7 LXX: ‘I myself who speak am here, like a season (ὥρα) upon the mountains’; Cyril reads ὥρα as springtime, so Pass B says ‘springtime’ (Hebrew reads ‘How beautiful upon the mountains’). Isaiah 33:20: Cyril has plural πόλεις πλουσίας where LXX has singular; kept plural. Psalm 87:3 = LXX Psalm 86:3. ‘The end of the prophets and of the law’ alludes to Romans 10:4 (Cyril adds the prophets). ἔναυλον ἔχουσα = holding Christ ‘ringing in her ears’, i.e. vividly present; rendered ‘vividly present to her’. ‘The transgression in Adam’ and ‘sin that tyrannized over us all’ echo Romans 5:12–21 generally; only the explicit Romans 5:14 clause is cited. ‘The kingdom long awaited’ not cited. Ends with the colon that introduces God’s command quoted at the start of §6 (Exodus 40:3–8). The old English placed ‘(Matthew 16:18)’ at this colon; corrected.

title: Where each holy vessel stands: the veil, the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies
english: Cyril: ‘And you shall set the ark of the testimony in place, and you shall cover the ark with the veil. And you shall bring in the table, and set out its bread of presentation. And you shall bring in the lampstand, and put its lamps on it. And you shall set the golden altar for burning incense before the ark. And you shall put the covering curtain on the door of the tent of testimony, and you shall set the altar of whole burnt offerings beside the doors of the tent of testimony. And you shall enclose the tent, and set all that belongs to it round about’ (Exodus 40:3–8). In these words one can see the sacred vessels brought into the holy tent, but not yet clearly the place that suits each one and was assigned to it. Would you like us, then, to gather from the commands about the tent a detailed and exact knowledge of these matters?
Palladius: Most gladly.

Cyril: God, then, said to the holy Moses: ‘And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and spun fine linen; you shall make it a woven work with cherubim. And you shall hang it on four pillars that cannot rot, overlaid with gold; their capitals shall be gold, and their four bases silver. And you shall put the veil on the pillars, and there, inside the veil, you shall bring in the ark of the testimony; and the veil shall divide for you between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. You shall cover the ark of the testimony with the veil in the Holy of Holies. And you shall set the table outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite the table on the south side of the tent; and you shall put the table on the north side of the tent. And you shall make a screen for the door of the tent, of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and twisted fine linen, the work of an embroiderer. And you shall make five pillars for the curtain and overlay them with gold; their capitals shall be gold, and you shall cast five bronze bases for them’ (Exodus 26:31–37). So much for these things. About the laver he says something like this: ‘Make a bronze laver, and a bronze base for it, for washing; and you shall put it between the tent of testimony and the altar’ (Exodus 30:18). Is the meaning of each point clear to you?
Palladius: Not at all. I am quite at a loss, I assure you, and I cannot say what it means.

Cyril: Then for each of the passages before us I will take hold of what bears on their spiritual meaning, and give an account as clear and distinct as I am able. The holy tent, Palladius, was set up in the wilderness with a twofold arrangement and form, as it were. One part was the innermost, and its name was the Holy of Holies. Around it, like a kind of entrance hall, was the first part, called the Holy Place (Hebrews 9:2–3). In the innermost tent the ark had been placed, and it had a curtain about it, hung on four golden pillars and skillfully made of blue and purple and twisted scarlet and spun fine linen.
translator_notes: Opening quotation is Exodus 40:3–8 in the LXX form, which lacks the laver verse (Hebrew/English 40:7); the range is given in English numbering. προθήσεις τὴν πρόθεσιν αὐτῆς: πρόθεσις here is the bread set out on the table (LXX ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως, Exodus 25:30; 40:23), so Pass B says ‘bread of presentation’. The last clause (περιθήσεις τὴν σκηνήν, καὶ πάντα τὰ αὐτῆς περιθήσεις κύκλῳ) differs from the standard LXX/Hebrew (which speak of the court or of consecrating); rendered literally as ‘enclose the tent, and set all that belongs to it round about’. The long quotation is Exodus 26:31–37 LXX; ὑάκινθος rendered ‘blue’; κόκκινον κεκλωσμένον ‘twisted scarlet’; βύσσος νενησμένη ‘spun fine linen’ and βύσσος κεκλωσμένη ‘twisted fine linen’, kept distinct as in Cyril’s text; ἄσηπτοι στῦλοι ‘pillars that cannot rot’ (no wood is named in this text). ἐπίσπαστρον ‘screen’. In 26:37 Cyril has τῷ καταπετάσματι (‘for the curtain’), which here means the door screen; rendered ‘curtain’ to keep the Greek word distinct from the inner veil. Laver: Exodus 30:18. ‘The first … called the Holy Place’ and ‘Holy of Holies’ follow Hebrews 9:2–3 closely (ἡ πρώτη … ἥτις λέγεται Ἅγια), so cited. θεωρία rendered ‘spiritual meaning’. The section ends with the two letters Εἰ- of the participle Εἰρηκότες, which runs across the column break; the whole word is translated at the start of §7, so nothing is lost or repeated.

title: The veil is Christ's flesh; the four pillars are the evangelists; the Word hidden until the resurrection
english: Cyril: We have already spoken, and sufficiently, I think, about the linen and the purple, the twisted scarlet, and the blue as well, so we will set repetition aside. But this much we will say for the present: the veil on four golden pillars with silver bases was then a hint of the mystery of Christ. Why so? Did not the wise Paul also name the body of Christ a veil for us, when he said: ‘the new and living way which he opened for us through the veil, that is, his flesh’ (Hebrews 10:20)?
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: See, then, as in shadows and riddles, how the Word, who is God and from God the Father by nature, came to be as in a golden and incorruptible ark, that is, in the temple taken from the Virgin; for the body of Christ is incorruptible and precious. And by taking the flesh he was all but hidden, as though behind a veil. We say that the Word from God was hidden, not as though he were confined within a small body, for the Son is everywhere and in all things, but because he remained unnoticed, in keeping with the plan of salvation, and waited for the time of his showing forth. And the time of his showing forth to all was his return to life from the dead. For before the precious cross he ordered the holy disciples not to make him known (Matthew 16:20); so it is written. But after he had suffered death and come back to life, he says: ‘Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19). So the veil hung on the pillars, covering the ark within; and it would be a type of Christ, who is lifted up on high by the preaching of the holy evangelists and is seen in the glory of the Godhead by those in the holy tent, that is, in the Church. The pillars are four, golden and set in silver; and the evangelists are equal to them in number, bright and precious. So the ark lay there, and the veil of linen and purple and the rest, reaching from top to bottom, kept it out of sight. Above the veil and above the cherubim on the right and on the left, God uttered his oracles, showing that he is above all creation. Even the highest of all rational beings, that is, the Seraphim, are seated beneath the divine glory beyond words, and they attend the Son himself as his guard of honor, even though he became flesh (John 1:14) and, insofar as he is man, came perhaps into a kind of lowering of his equality with the Father. That is why he himself said: ‘My Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28). Yet being equal by nature to the One who begot him, he says that he came into a lesser state, and this only because of his humanity. For this reason, in the holy tent too, the cherubim were around the veil, they too attending the Son as God. And above the veil itself, which stood as a type of Christ, God is understood to be. For he says: ‘And I will make myself known from there, and I will speak with you’ (Exodus 25:22). For the Father is beyond all creation, and beyond Emmanuel himself, not insofar as Emmanuel is understood to be God and is God, for he is equal to God in all things, but insofar as
translator_notes: Opens with the participle Εἰρηκότες split at the column break (Εἰ- at the end of §6); translated whole here. Hebrews 10:20 is quoted as Paul’s, following Cyril’s attribution. ‘He ordered the holy disciples not to make him known’: the sense matches Matthew 16:20 (also Mark 8:30, Luke 9:21), cited there; the wording ἵνα μὴ φανερὸν αὐτὸν ποιῶσι echoes Matthew 12:16 and Mark 3:12, where the command is to the crowds and the spirits. ‘For it is written thus’ (Γέγραπται γὰρ ὡδί) is followed by no quotation in the PG text; a quotation may have dropped out, or the phrase may simply point to the Gospel account. Rendered ‘so it is written’ and nothing is supplied. ‘The temple taken from the Virgin’ may recall John 2:21 and ‘incorruptible body’ Psalm 16:10 / Acts 2:27; both too loose to cite. ‘Seraphim’ is Cyril’s word here (not ‘cherubim’), kept; the image may recall Isaiah 6:2, not cited. ‘He became flesh’ is John 1:14. ὡς ἐν ὑφέσει τυχὸν τῆς πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα ἰσότητος, καθὸ πέφυκεν ἄνθρωπος: Cyril hedges twice (ὡς, τυχόν) and limits the lowering to the humanity; Pass B keeps ‘perhaps’, ‘a kind of’ and ‘insofar as he is man’. ‘My Father is greater than I’ is John 14:28 (Cyril adds μου). Possible echo of Philippians 2:6 in ‘equal by nature’, not cited. ‘I will make myself known from there, and I will speak with you’ is Exodus 25:22 LXX (also Exodus 30:6). ἐχρημάτιζε rendered ‘gave his answers’ (oracular speech). οἰκονομικῶς rendered ‘in keeping with the plan of salvation’. The section ends mid-sentence at ἀλλ’ ὅσον; §8 continues ‘he came into the form of a servant and the measure of humanity’ (Philippians 2:7, to be cited in §8). Pass B therefore ends with ‘but insofar as’ and no full stop.

title: The incense altar, the lampstand and the table
english: Cyril: …came into the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and into the measure of humanity.
Palladius: How subtle and deep your argument is.
Cyril: And yet it does not stray from the point.
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: With the ark set in this way, Scripture says, ‘And you shall set the golden altar for burning incense opposite the ark’ (Exodus 40:5). I think we have already said enough to show that Christ is the golden altar. Yet it was set opposite the ark, over which hung the veil, with the seraphim around it and God above, as though God were receiving the incomparable fragrance of Emmanuel. For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, as it is written (1 Peter 2:22). That is why he himself said, ‘The Father loves the Son’ (John 3:35; John 5:20). And we ourselves are also acceptable to God when we are fragrant with the ointment of Christ. Paul too will confirm this when he writes, ‘But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us makes known the fragrance of the knowledge of him; for we are the fragrance of Christ to God’ (2 Corinthians 2:14–15).
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: Let us consider carefully, then, with our eyes fixed on what is written, that the ark was placed on the side of the holy tent that faces southwest and west, and opposite it the golden altar, in the place that faces the rising sun. For east and west are filled with Christ, and north and south as well. So too the lampstand’s place was the south side of the tent, and the table’s the side toward the north (Exodus 26:35). We have already shown at length that Christ is signified by both: the lampstand shows that Christ is light, and the table with what lay on it shows that he is life and the living bread (John 6:51). But consider this, and look closely at the mystery. The land of the Jews lies farthest to the south, while the land of the Gentiles lies further to the north. So from where the two stood, I mean the lampstand and the table, those who wish to understand well will surely gather that Christ shone as light on the Jews and proclaimed among them, ‘I am the light’ (John 8:12). For he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24), and ‘theirs are the promises’, as the Scriptures say (Romans 9:4). But since they did not accept the light of the truth, he became for the Gentiles life and bread from heaven (John 6:33). Nor are the Gentiles without light; you may learn this too from the way the light of the lampstand reached the north side of the tent as well. And since the holy tent was very narrow, it is not unlikely that the lampstand seemed almost to stand beside the table, even though it held the southern place. The figure also shows us in another way that, when the divine light shines out, the worthy may be able to share in Christ as the living and true bread. The Gentiles have become members of one body with Christ and sharers in him (Ephesians 3:6). And again the inspired Paul writes: the Gentiles have become members of one body and sharers…
translator_notes: PG 68.664. Opens mid-sentence: §7 ends ἀλλ' ὅσον ('but only so far as'); this row renders only ἧκεν εἰς δούλου μορφήν... and keeps the Cyril label with an ellipsis. Exodus 40:5 matches the LXX wording exactly (Exodus 30:6 gives the same placement in other words). 'Not commit sin ... no deceit in His mouth' follows 1 Peter 2:22 (itself from Isaiah 53:9); cited to 1 Peter. The words ‘The Father loves the Son’ match John 3:35 exactly (ἀγαπᾷ), but Cyril gives them to Christ himself (αὐτός, as in §7), and in John 3:35 the speaker is John the Baptist or the evangelist; Christ says the same in John 5:20 (φιλεῖ), so both are cited (reviewer). 2 Corinthians 2:14: Migne prints δι' ἡμᾶς ('on our account') where the New Testament has δι' ἡμῶν ('through us'); rendered 'through us' as the evident sense, the Migne form may be a print slip. Cyril says seraphim stand around the ark (here and in §7), where Exodus has cherubim; kept as written. Ark 'toward λίψ and west': λίψ is the south-west wind, and in the LXX often 'south'; rendered 'southwest and west'. πρὸς ἀκτῖνα ('toward the ray') rendered 'faces the rising sun', the east. Lampstand south and table north follow Exodus 26:35 (also 40:22–24); Cyril paraphrases, so the citation marks an allusion, not a quotation. 'East and west ... north and south filled with Christ': possible echo of Psalm 107:3 or Malachi 1:11, too loose to cite. 'They did not accept the light' may echo John 1:11 or 3:19; not cited. 'Living and true bread' echoes John 6:32 and 6:51 (6:51 already cited above). Ephesians 3:6 has σύσσωμα καὶ συμμέτοχα; Cyril adapts it twice in a row: once as his own statement ('sharers of Christ'), then 'Paul writes again', followed in §9 by 'sharers of light', which is not Paul's wording. The repetition may be a dittography in the print or a lost quotation; both statements are translated as printed, without quotation marks on the second. The sentence breaks at γέ|γονε and continues in §9.

title: The door screen, the five pillars, and the law at the threshold
english: Cyril: …in light, the spiritual light, that is, and they are filled still further, ‘as the day dawns and the Morning Star rises’ in the mind (2 Peter 1:19), as one of the Savior’s disciples said. With the things in the Holy of Holies placed and made in this way, he commanded that a drawn curtain, or veil, be made of blue, purple, spun scarlet and twisted fine linen; and he said that it must be stretched across the entrances of the tent, hung on five golden pillars whose bases were bronze (Exodus 26:36–37). He calls the hanging over the door a ‘drawn curtain’ because, I think, it was drawn back on slender rings when the entrance was to be opened, and then drawn across again and spread over the doorway to hide the Holy Place. The five pillars, golden and bound with bronze, prefigure the teachers and leaders of the Churches who belong, as it were, to the fifth period of time, the period in which the coming of Christ took place. Rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15), they are precious as gold and ring out clearly like bronze. ‘For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’ (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18). Through their skilled teaching of the mysteries, inspired by God, they also widen, as it were, the entrances for those who wish to hasten into the Holy of Holies. The Holy of Holies, then, that is, the inner tent, was covered by the veil. The first tent was set right against the second and joined to it. It held the altar of burnt offerings, on which every offering made with blood was carried out, the cakes and the frankincense, and every sacrifice and drink offering; and it held the bronze laver as well, beside the altar (Exodus 30:18). The altar’s place was by the doors of the tent, clearly the outer tent (Exodus 40:6), and the laver’s place was the very middle of the tent.
Palladius: And what, again, are we to understand by this careful arrangement?

Cyril: Holy Scripture is exact, Palladius, and nothing at all in it is idle. See how the figure has shown us the law as a tutor leading us to Christ (Galatians 3:24). For the altar of the worship under the law was set right at the entrances that lead into the Holy of Holies. For the law barely brings us as far as the beginnings of the mysteries of Christ, to what are, as it were, the first entrances of exact knowledge about him; but it does not bring us at all into the Holy of Holies, that is, into the inner tent, where Christ is found in many forms: as the Word of God, as light, as living bread, as a sweet fragrance to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2). Or would you not say that the preparatory practice of worship under the law was the elements and first principles of the oracles of God (Hebrews 5:12)?
Palladius: That is true.
Cyril: That the law made nothing perfect (Hebrews 7:19), for ‘it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away…
translator_notes: PG 68.665. Opens mid-sentence (γέ|γονε from §8); Cyril label kept with an ellipsis. 2 Peter 1:19 is adapted: Cyril writes κατὰ νοῦν ('in the mind') where Peter has 'in your hearts'; Φωσφόρος is capitalized as Christ. Door screen: Exodus 26:36–37 (LXX ἐπίσπαστρον, five pillars, bronze bases); Cyril swaps the participles (κοκκίνου κεκλωσμένου, βύσσου νενησμένης) against the LXX; rendered 'spun scarlet and twisted fine linen'. δικνουμένης is doubtful: no such verb is attested in this sense; it may stand for διανοιγομένης ('being opened'), and the rendering 'when the entrance was to be opened' follows that guess. ἀνόπιν rendered 'back'. 'Fifth period' (πέμπτῳ καιρῷ): Cyril's scheme of ages in which Christ comes in the fifth; a link to the parable of the workers (Matthew 20) is possible but not cited. 'Ring out like bronze' may recall 1 Corinthians 13:1 but in a positive sense; not cited. Psalm citation: Cyril quotes Psalm 18:5 LXX, which is Psalm 19:4 in English Bibles; Romans 10:18 quotes the same words of the apostles' preaching, and Cyril applies them to teachers in the same way, so both are cited. 'First tent' here holds the altar of burnt offering and the laver, so Cyril means the court, not the Holy Place of Exodus; kept as written. Altar by the doors of the tent: Exodus 40:6 (LXX θυσιαστήριον τῶν καρπωμάτων παρὰ τὰς θύρας). Bronze laver beside the altar: Exodus 30:18 (between the tent and the altar; also Exodus 40:7 Hebrew). ἐπιτήρησις rendered 'careful arrangement' (literally 'close observance'). Galatians 3:24 (law as παιδαγωγὸς εἰς Χριστόν). εὐωδίας ὀσμή of Christ to God: Ephesians 5:2 is the one New Testament verse that says this of Christ, so it is cited. Hebrews 5:12: τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ Θεοῦ. Hebrews 7:19 (οὐδὲν ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος) is a clear allusion. The Hebrews 10:4 quotation breaks at ἁμαρ|τίας and its citation is placed in §10 where the quotation closes. Reviewer: ἐπίσπαστρον rendered 'drawn curtain' (from ἐπισπάω, 'draw over') so that Cyril's explanation of the name, that it was drawn back and drawn across, reads naturally in English.

title: The laver as baptism, the veiled law, and Paul on the two tents
english: Cyril: …sins’ (Hebrews 10:4), you can learn at once, and with no trouble at all, once you have considered what the laver was for. It stood in the middle of the first tent, bright and plain to see, washing beforehand with water those who were going into the Holy of Holies; for the law on this point was laid down for the priests (Exodus 30:19–21). So even what seemed to be fulfillment under the law was incomplete; it pointed to the cleansing through holy baptism, which washes the sacred race clean. I mean the race of those justified by faith, whom the inspired disciple addressed when he said, ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the praises of him who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light’ (1 Peter 2:9). One should also know that a veil was stretched across the door of the outer tent as well, so that the Holy Place, that is, the first tent, where the altar of the law stood, would not lie bare and open to those outside. Here again, I think, the figure shows that the law itself is not plain to just anyone. For the letter has a veil over it (2 Corinthians 3:14), and is in a way covered and wrapped in the obscurity that belongs to shadows.
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: In the first tent, then, stood the laver and the altar; in the second and innermost stood the ark and the lampstand, and also the golden censer with the fine incense upon it, and the table and the loaves. The inspired Paul also mentions a golden jar holding the manna (Hebrews 9:4). He names Aaron’s rod too, which he says was laid up in the Holy of Holies, since he was well versed in the sacred Scriptures and knew very well what had been decreed at various times and what God had commanded blessed Moses. Yet he knows that the table and the lampstand were in the first tent (Hebrews 9:2). He writes this about the two covenants: ‘In speaking of a new covenant he has made the first old; and what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish. Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly sanctuary. For a tent was prepared, the first one, in which were the lampstand and the table and the setting out of the loaves; it is called the Holy Place. Behind the second veil was the tent called the Holy of Holies, which had a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which were a golden jar holding the manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat’, of which we cannot now speak in detail (Hebrews 8:13–9:5).
Palladius: Suppose, then, that someone chose to be inquisitive and said we ought to give the reasons for the whole arrangement. What answer would we give?
Cyril: The reason, Palladius, is that he commanded some of these things to be done before the holy tent was built, and others after it. For in Exodus, even…
translator_notes: PG 68.668. Opens mid-word (ἁμαρ|τίας from §9); Cyril label kept with an ellipsis; the Hebrews 10:4 citation sits here where the quotation closes. Law of washing for the priests: Exodus 30:19–21 (also 40:30–32). πλήρωσις ('fulfillment') is odd beside a laver; πλύσις ('washing') would read more easily, but the printed word is translated and the doubt recorded. ἱερὸν γένος rendered 'sacred race' (ἱερός, not ἱερατικός). 1 Peter 2:9: Cyril has ἡμᾶς ('called us') where the New Testament has ὑμᾶς ('you'); 'us' is kept. Veil at the door of the outer tent: since Cyril's 'outer' or 'first' tent holds the altar of burnt offering, this may be the screen of the court gate (Exodus 27:16), or the tent-door screen already described in §9 (Exodus 26:36); Cyril gives no verse and the identification is doubtful, so no inline citation (reviewer removed Exodus 27:16). 'The letter has a covering': 2 Corinthians 3:14 (the veil over the reading of the old covenant), a clear allusion. Cyril places the lampstand, censer, table and loaves in the inner tent, then notes that Paul puts table and lampstand in the first tent; Palladius' question and Cyril's answer about the order of the commands deal with this difference. θυμιατήριον rendered 'golden censer' to keep it apart from the θυσιαστήριον ('altar') of §8; many versions of Hebrews 9:4 render it 'golden altar of incense'. Hebrews quotation runs from 8:13 to 9:5; Migne closes the quotation marks before περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἔστι νῦν λέγειν κατὰ μέρος, but these are also the closing words of Hebrews 9:5, which Cyril takes over as his own, so the citation is placed after them. ἅγιον κοσμικόν rendered 'earthly sanctuary'. 'He commanded' (προστέταχεν): the subject is God, unstated in the Greek. The sentence breaks at καίτοι | πρὶν ὅλως and continues in §11 ('even before the patterns ... were shown at all').

title: The order of the types, and the manna as Christ
english: Cyril: …before the patterns of the holy tent had been shown at all, and the commands about it given, God uttered the oracle about the golden jar (Exodus 16:32–34), since he knew what was to come. After the whole tent had been set up, we shall find in Numbers that Aaron’s rod was brought into the Holy of Holies (Numbers 17:10). And in Leviticus God gave further laws about the lampstand and the table in the first tent (Leviticus 24:1–9). And Paul, most wise and learned in the law, leaves out nothing at all of what took place, but recalls the first things, the middle ones and the last.
Palladius: Very well said. Then explain each thing clearly and point by point; for surely there is a deep meaning in them.

Cyril: Yes, you are right; for that is how the matter truly stands. I will make the jar the starting point of my account. God sent the manna down like rain on the people of Israel in the wilderness; for this was their food and bread from above, from heaven (Exodus 16:4). But what was done did not stop at things of sense. As through a type and a shadow, it leads us up to understand that in due time the Word would come to us from above and from the Father, as bread from heaven, just as the divine David hints to us when he says: ‘He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels’ (Psalm 78:24–25). We certainly do not say that the physical manna was the bread from heaven and of angels. For a spirit is fed spiritually, and a body according to its own nature, that is, bodily. The food of angels, the bread fit for the heavens and for the spirits above, is the Word who is from God the Father. So the manna signified Christ. Yet the type is of no use unless the truth has been received. For it is a shadow of the truth, not made chiefly for its own sake, but so that it might paint in itself a picture of something better. That is why Christ gave the crowds of the Jews a wise rebuke, because they admired, not him as the truth, but Moses, the servant of the types. For he said: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, Moses has given you the manna; but the bread of God is he who came down from heaven and gives life to the world. I am the living bread’ (John 6:32–33, 51). So it was in making the manna an image of the Word who came down from above, from heaven, that God gave the oracle about the jar. It is written thus: ‘And Moses said: This is the word which the Lord commanded: Fill the omer with manna, to be laid up for your generations, so that they may see the bread which you ate in the wilderness, when the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt. And Moses said to Aaron: Take one golden jar, and put into it a full omer of manna, and lay it up before God, to be kept for your generations, as the Lord commanded Moses. And Aaron laid it up before the testimony, to be kept’ (Exodus 16:32–34). For just as we were saying that the ark, holding the divine word, signified Emmanuel, since the Word of God was within, as in a…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, continuing §10 (‘For in Exodus, even…’); the subject of κατεχρησμῴδησε is God (named in §10’s frame), supplied in English. Psalm 78:24–25 is LXX Psalm 77:24–25 (English numbering given). Exodus 16:33: the LXX adds ‘golden’ (στάμνον χρυσοῦν) where the Hebrew has only ‘a jar’; Cyril follows the LXX; γομόρ rendered ‘omer’. John 6:32–33, 51: the printed text is a free paraphrase and lacks the ‘not’ of John 6:32 (οὐ Μωϋσῆς δέδωκεν); translated as printed, without restoring the negation; its γάρ is rendered ‘but’ because the clause contrasts the manna with the bread of God. ‘The living bread’ matches John 6:51 (ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν), not 6:35. ‘The divine word’ (θεῖον λόγον) held by the ark means the tablets of the law; lower case to keep it apart from the Word (Λόγος) in the next clause, where Cyril plays on the two. ‘Numbers’ refers to Numbers 17:10 (LXX 17:25), where Aaron’s rod is laid up before the testimony; Cyril’s ‘Holy of Holies’ is his reading, following Hebrews 9:4. ‘Leviticus’ = Leviticus 24:1–9 (lamp oil, twelve loaves), quoted in §14. Paul’s summary of the tent (Hebrews 9:1–5) was quoted in §10 and is not cited again here. Reviewer: ‘like rain … bread from above, from heaven’ alludes to Exodus 16:4 (LXX ὕω ὑμῖν ἄρτους ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ), now cited inline. τὸ μάννα τὸ αἰσθητόν rendered ‘the physical manna’ (here and in §12) instead of ‘the manna of sense’.

title: The full jar before the Father; Korah’s revolt and the twelve rods
english: Cyril: …holy temple, I mean the temple that came from the Virgin; in the same way the golden jar, bearing within it the physical manna, shows us the life-giving Word from above, plainly the Word who is from the Father, as in a holy and undefiled body. And the jar was full to the brim with manna; for ‘in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily’ (Colossians 2:9), in the words of blessed Paul. And ‘he does not give the Spirit by measure’ (John 3:34). For Christ is perfect in every way. The jar was laid up to be kept for the generations of the sons of Israel (Exodus 16:33); for Christ is incorruptible, abides for ever, and is well known in every season and age. And he is before the Lord, that is, in the eyes of the Father. For when the Only Begotten became one of us, he then also entered into the Holy of Holies through the greater and more perfect tent (Hebrews 9:11–12), that is, into heaven, ‘now to appear in the presence of God for us’ (Hebrews 9:24), as it is written. For it is not himself he sets in the Father’s sight, but us, as in himself, though we had fallen from his presence and, as it were, out of his sight, through the transgression in Adam and the sin that ruled as a tyrant over all. So in Christ we have gained access, and boldness to enter the holy place (Ephesians 3:12; Hebrews 10:19), as wise Paul has told us. For just as we have been raised with him and seated with him in the heavenly places in Christ (Ephesians 2:6), so again in him we have come into the presence of the Father. Let this be enough about the sacred jar. Now come, let us show that Aaron’s rod too signifies Christ, if you agree.
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: Korah, then, and Abiram too, and Dathan besides, sprang from the tribe and blood of Levi. Though they had been entrusted, Scripture says, with a ministry in the holy tent appointed by decree from above, they thirsted for the glory of Moses and Aaron, seizing the honour for themselves, although God had not called them to it (Numbers 16:8–11; Hebrews 5:4). What is more, swelling with savage insolence and exceedingly proud, they poured out on them both abuse that could no longer be borne and was utterly intolerable. Like bulls that scorn the herd they broke away, and shaking off their service under God, they persuaded others to break loose with them into impiety. But they paid the penalty for what they had dared. For the earth opened its mouth and sent that arrogant people down to Hades, with their own kin, their tents and their goods (Numbers 16:31–33). Then the Lawgiver, wishing to make plain that Aaron had received the chief rank in the priesthood by decree from above and not by the wishes of Moses, said to the most excellent Moses (Numbers 17:2–3): ‘Speak to the sons of Israel, and take from them a rod for each father’s house, from all their leaders according to their fathers’ houses, twelve rods; and write each man’s name on his rod. And write Aaron’s name on the rod of Levi; for there is one rod. According to the tribe of their fathers’ houses they shall…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, continuing the ark–jar comparison from §11. ὠδίνουσα (‘travailing with’) rendered ‘bearing within it’; the birth image echoes ‘the temple taken from the Virgin’. Colossians 2:9: Cyril has the aorist ἐνῴκησε (‘dwelt’) for the New Testament’s present κατοικεῖ. John 3:34 cited as quoted (‘he does not give the Spirit by measure’). Καὶ ἔστιν ἔναντι Κυρίου: subject read as Christ (the antitype of the jar), in line with the next sentence; it could also mean ‘it [the jar] stands before the Lord’. Hebrews 9:11–12 and 9:24 are cited separately because Cyril joins the ‘greater and more perfect tent’ to the quoted phrase ‘now to appear in the presence of God for us’. Access and boldness: προσαγωγή and παρρησία together match Ephesians 3:12; ‘boldness to enter the holy place’ (εἰς τὴν εἴσοδον τῶν ἁγίων) is Hebrews 10:19; Cyril attributes Hebrews to Paul, kept as he says it. Korah narrative: Numbers 16 (LXX numbering is the same for 16:1–35). Cyril says Dathan and Abiram were also of Levi, but Numbers 16:1 makes them Reubenites; translated as he says it, not corrected. ‘Seizing the honour … God had not called them to it’ alludes to Hebrews 5:4 (τὴν τιμήν … καλούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ). ‘Like bulls that scorn the herd’ (ἀτιμαγέλαι ταῦροι) is a classical image, not Scripture; not cited. ‘The Lawgiver’ (ὁ νομοθέτης) means God here, so it is capitalised. The rod quotation is Numbers 17:2–3 in English numbering = LXX Numbers 17:17–18; the section breaks inside the verb δώσουσι, so the English ends on ‘they shall…’ and §13 opens with ‘…give them’. Reviewer: the rod quotation had no inline citation in this section; ‘(Numbers 17:2–3)’ is now placed at the words that introduce it, since the section ends inside the quotation.

title: Aaron’s rod blossoms: Christ the High Priest rises from death
english: Cyril: …give them. And you shall set them in the tent of witness, before the testimony, where I will make myself known to you. And the rod of the man whom I choose shall sprout; and I will take away from me the grumbling of the sons of Israel, which they grumble against you. And Moses spoke to the sons of Israel, and all their leaders gave him a rod, one rod for each leader, according to their fathers’ houses, twelve rods; and Aaron’s rod was among their rods. And Moses laid up the rods before the Lord in the tent of witness. And on the next day Moses and Aaron went into the tent of witness; and behold, Aaron’s rod for the house of Levi had sprouted, and put forth a shoot, and burst into flower, and borne almonds. And Moses brought out all the rods from the presence of the Lord to all the sons of Israel; and they looked, and each man took his own rod. And the Lord said to Moses: Lay up Aaron’s rod before the testimonies, to be kept as a sign for the sons of the disobedient; and let their grumbling against me cease, so that they do not die’ (Numbers 17:3–10). So the blossoming of the rod was no obscure sign that the inspired Aaron, as one of the blood of Levi, had been chosen with distinction and set apart for the priestly service. But when the account is turned once more to spiritual contemplation, the mystery of Christ will shine out again, though still, as it were, in very coarse types.
Palladius: In what way?

Cyril: Emmanuel has been appointed for us by God the Father as Lawgiver and High Priest at once, to offer himself for us as the sacrifice. For as blessed Paul said: ‘The law through Moses appoints as high priests men who have weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son made perfect for ever’ (Hebrews 7:28). So the Word came down from heaven and became one of us, ‘a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tent, which the Lord pitched, and not man’ (Hebrews 8:2). But those of the blood of Israel did not see fit to think rightly. Setting their own will against him, as it were, they shot at him in many ways with the arrows of envy, no longer holding back their tongues, their insolence or their outrageous schemes; and the wretches, destroying themselves, at last crucified him. Yet the rod from the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1) blossomed again. For Christ sprang up again and came back to life, ‘having loosed the pangs of death’ (Acts 2:24), as it is written. Since he is Life by nature, as God, how could he be held by death (Acts 2:24), and not rather triumph over corruption? Just as the springing up of the rod, when wood already past flowering unexpectedly sprouted again, was a sufficient sign to the people of old that Aaron had been appointed high priest by decree from above, so we say that his trampling on death and coming back to life as befits God is a clear, plain and fully sufficient proof that Emmanuel is also God by nature. Indeed Christ himself, although…
translator_notes: Opens mid-word (δώ|σουσι), finishing the quotation begun in §12. Numbers 17:3–10 in English numbering = LXX Numbers 17:18–25 (‘…give them’ ends 17:3 = LXX 17:18) (the LXX counts English 16:36–50 as 17:1–15). κάρυα means ‘nuts’ in Greek; rendered ‘almonds’ with the Hebrew and the English Bibles, which also prepares for the almond rod of Jeremiah 1:11 in §14. σημεῖον τοῖς υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνηκόων rendered ‘a sign for the sons of the disobedient’ (Hebrew: ‘rebels’). καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀποθάνωσι rendered ‘so that they do not die’; the strong negation is kept. ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς with κεχειροτόνηται rendered ‘for us’ (it could also be ‘over us’). ‘Lawgiver’ is capitalised as a title of Christ next to ‘High Priest’. Hebrews 7:28: Cyril adds ‘through Moses’ (διὰ Μωσέως) and attributes Hebrews to Paul; both kept. Hebrews 8:2: τῶν ἁγίων rendered ‘the sanctuary’. Isaiah 11:1 LXX has ῥάβδος (‘rod’) from the root of Jesse, which is why Cyril links it to Aaron’s rod; ‘rod’ kept to keep the link. Acts 2:24 is quoted (‘having loosed the pangs of death’) and then alluded to (‘how could he be held by death’), so it is cited at both places. ἐν τύποις ἔτι παχυτάτοις: ‘very coarse types’ (παχύς, thick, gross) means figures still thick and material, not yet transparent. ‘Did not see fit to think rightly’ renders οὐκ ἐδόκει φρονεῖν ὀρθά. No citation is given for the crucifixion summary, which is narrative and not a quotation. Reviewer: προσκομιῶν is a future participle of purpose, so ‘to offer himself’ replaces ‘offering himself’.

title: The sign of Jonah, the almond rod, and the lamp and loaves
english: Cyril: …he was able to accomplish, without effort and with ease, anything whatever beyond what is likely or reasonable, he said to those who were asking for a sign: ‘This generation is evil; it asks for a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights’ (Matthew 12:39–40). So the sign that the Son is God by nature and was begotten of God the Father, a sign truly renowned and plain to all and enough to bring the truly fair-minded to faith, is this: he abolished death and corruption and blossomed again into life. ‘For he has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep’ (1 Corinthians 15:20) ‘and the firstborn from the dead’ (Colossians 1:18). And the sign has been given to the sons of the disobedient (Numbers 17:10), so that they may know that Christ has become high priest over us by the vote of God the Father, ‘holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens’ (Hebrews 7:26), as it is written.
Palladius: Well, Aaron’s rod did blossom for us; the sacred word has just shown us that. But it blossomed with almonds (Numbers 17:8), and I cannot make out what the riddle is.

Cyril: In the first place, Palladius, there is nothing unlikely in supposing that the rod was cut from an almond tree; it was the custom among the people of old to use staffs of this kind as well. But if we must also fit to it an explanation suited to spiritual contemplation, I would mention in turn something that is widely repeated, and that seems to some people worth believing: that a rod of almond wood is not without power to cause sleeplessness if it is laid near a person’s head, perhaps producing this effect through natural powers, by the will of God. And he who knows all things, the Maker of the universe, will in some way confirm this for us himself when he says to Jeremiah: ‘What do you see, Jeremiah?’ And Jeremiah said, ‘A staff of almond wood.’ To this God says: ‘You have seen rightly, for I am keeping watch over my words, to perform them’ (Jeremiah 1:11–12). The almond rod, then, would fittingly be understood as a symbol of sleeplessness. And Christ’s return to life from the dead was an awakening, as if from sleep. That is why he also says through the lyre of the Psalmist: ‘I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord upheld me’ (Psalm 3:5).
Palladius: What you say is true.

Cyril: About the lamp and the table in the first tent, it is written again as follows: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the sons of Israel, and let them take pure oil, beaten, for the light, to keep a lamp burning continually outside the veil in the tent of witness. And Aaron and his sons shall burn it from evening until morning before the Lord continually, a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations. On the pure lampstand you shall burn the lamps before the Lord until morning. And you shall take fine flour and make of it twelve…’ (Leviticus 24:1–5)
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: the subject ('Christ himself, although…') is at the end of §13 (PG 68.673), so the English begins with an ellipsis under Cyril's label. Jonah quotation: wording follows Matthew 12:39–40 ('the sign of Jonah the prophet', three days and three nights), but the opening 'This generation is evil; it asks for a sign' is closer to Luke 11:29; cited as Matthew only. 'Sons of the disobedient' (τοῖς υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνηκόων) echoes LXX Numbers 17:25 = English Numbers 17:10 (Aaron's rod kept as a sign for the rebels); cited at English numbering. Numbers 17:8 is LXX 17:23. 'By the vote of God the Father … high priest' may echo Hebrews 5:10 ('designated by God a high priest'); left uncited as an allusion of uncertain precision. κάρυα / καρυΐνη: Greek 'nut' / 'of nut wood'; rendered 'almond' because the LXX uses these words for the Hebrew shaqed (almond) in both Numbers 17:8 and Jeremiah 1:11, and English Bibles read 'almond' there. Cyril's argument rests on the Hebrew wordplay (shaqed 'almond' / shoqed 'watching') carried into the Greek as καρυΐνη / ἐγρήγορα; he presents the sleeplessness belief as popular report ('commonly repeated', 'some seem to accept'), and the English keeps that distance. ἐγρήγορα rendered 'I am keeping watch' to keep the link with 'sleeplessness' and 'awakening' (γρηγόρησις). Psalm 3:5 = LXX Psalm 3:6; Cyril reads the aorist ἀντελάβετο ('upheld') where the LXX has the future ἀντιλήψεται. Leviticus 24 quotation runs on into §15; the Greek quote omits ἐλάινον ('of olives') in 24:2, which Cyril supplies in his comment in §15. 'Tent of witness' = σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου.

title: Pure oil and the lamps: Christ's light in the Church and under the law
english: Cyril: …loaves. Each loaf shall be of two tenths, and you shall set them in two rows, six loaves to a row, on the pure table before the Lord. And you shall put pure frankincense and salt on the row, and these shall go with the loaves as a memorial, set before the Lord. On the Sabbath day you shall set them out before the Lord continually, in the presence of the sons of Israel, an everlasting covenant. And they shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place, for it is a most holy thing. This is his share from the offerings sacrificed to the Lord, a perpetual ordinance’ (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The oil, then, is pure, and it is olive oil besides: that is, it comes from olives, not from other, more earthy kinds of seed, which did yield pressed oil, but oil that was spurious and, so to speak, adulterated. For the light in the churches is always pure and truly genuine: the light, clearly, that comes through Christ, by the Spirit, even if it is ministered through the voice of the saints, to whom Christ said: ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14). And this is no wonder. For with those whom he called his brothers (Hebrews 2:11) and made partakers of himself (Hebrews 3:14), he would fittingly share the glory of his own honors as well.

So the lamp burns in the first tent as well, and the matter would have a twofold sense. In the inner tent seven lamps shine (Exodus 25:37); they are kindled in the morning, and they pour a rich light upon those who hurry in. And the lampstand was Christ, again as in a type, flooding with abundant and generous light those who wish to hurry into the Holy of Holies. For, it says, ‘Come to him and be enlightened’ (Psalm 34:5). Moreover, the lighting of the lamps in the morning would signify the time when he became man. For something like a day dawned, and a light perceived by the mind shone out, driving away the darkness of our ancient ignorance and scattering the mist that had fallen like night upon the hearts of all. So too the prophet called for the time of the Savior’s coming among us, when he said: ‘In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will keep watch’ (Psalm 5:3). For when would the prayers of all have become acceptable, and when would we who once wandered have stood, as it were, before God, through kinship with him (the spiritual kind, of course) and through obedience and faith, if the light from heaven, that is, Christ, had not shone upon us?

So in the inner tent the light of the seven lamps is rich and clear, but in the first tent it was a single lamp that gave light; and it showed, I think, that not even those being schooled under the law were without the divine light, as the thing itself makes plain. For the law given through Moses also called people out of the worship of many gods to the knowledge of him who is God by nature and in truth. It drew the people of old away from still serving the creation rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25), and persuaded them that they must hold fast to the Maker of all. And these things were not achieved in the souls of those under its schooling without the light perceived by the mind. So, to say it once more, the illumination that comes from Christ is rich and plentiful for those who enter the Holy of Holies, but less for those under the law; and the statement is true.
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation (Leviticus 24:5, 'twelve | loaves'), so the first paragraph begins with an ellipsis under Cyril's label; the whole section is one Cyril speech, split into natural paragraphs. 'And salt' in Leviticus 24:7 is an LXX plus (not in the Hebrew). Leviticus 24:9 Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων rendered 'a most holy thing' in the quotation, but 'the Holy of Holies' where Cyril uses the same phrase for the inner sanctuary. 'Olive oil besides' renders καὶ μὴν καὶ ἐλάϊνον: Cyril supplies the LXX ἐλάινον of Leviticus 24:2 that his quotation in §14 left out. κεκαπηλευμένον ('adulterated', literally 'hawked like a huckster's wine') may echo 2 Corinthians 2:17; uncited. 'Named his brothers … made partakers of himself' cited to Hebrews 2:11 and Hebrews 3:14 as clear Hebrews echoes (Cyril has just quoted Hebrews 7:26); not quotations. Seven lamps: Exodus 25:37 (also Numbers 8:2); Cyril places the seven-lamp lampstand in the 'inner tent' and the single lamp of Leviticus 24:2–4 in the 'first tent'; the English keeps his arrangement without correcting it. The lamps being 'kindled in the morning' is left uncited (compare Exodus 30:7–8, where Aaron tends the lamps morning and evening). Psalm 34:5 = LXX Psalm 33:6 ('Come to him and be enlightened'). Psalm 5:3 = LXX Psalm 5:4; ἐπόψομαι is first person with no object ('and I will look / keep watch'), rendered 'I will keep watch'. ἐνανθρώπησις rendered 'the time when he became man' (literally 'the becoming-man', i.e. the Incarnation). παρεκάλει ('called for, summoned') is kept as 'called for'; a scribal slip for παρεδήλου ('indicated') is possible but not assumed. 'The law given through Moses' may echo John 1:17; uncited as a common phrase. παιδαγωγούμενοι ('being schooled') recalls Galatians 3:24 (the law as tutor); uncited. Διηύγασε ('it dawned') may echo 2 Peter 1:19; uncited.

title: The lamp as John the Baptist, the twelve loaves as the apostles
english: Cyril: …For in spiritual brightness the shadow in the law (Hebrews 10:1) is in no way equal to the decrees of the Gospel. These flash their light around the whole inhabited world, while the shadow was a token for those of Israel alone.
Palladius: You have spoken rightly.
Cyril: It seems, Palladius, that the table and the lamp in the first tent point to something else as well.
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: The lamp, perhaps, is John, the inspired Baptist, while the twelve loaves prefigure for us the company of the holy apostles.
Palladius: In what way?

Cyril: Or do you not know that for those under the law in Judea the inspired Baptist was a kind of lamp going before Christ, and that God the Father spoke of him beforehand: ‘I have prepared a lamp for my Christ’ (Psalm 132:17)? The Savior himself also bore witness to this, saying of him to the teachers of the Jews: ‘He was the lamp that burns and shines, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light’ (John 5:35). See how blessed Paul, as one learned in the law, all but calls to mind the lamp in the first tent (Hebrews 9:2). For the lawgiver commanded that it must be kept unquenched, saying: ‘And Aaron and his sons shall burn it from evening until morning before the Lord continually’ (Leviticus 24:3). Yet the Jews took delight in John for a very short time, in that they ran to the baptism he gave and marveled greatly at him; then they put the ever-shining lamp to sleep in death, all but quenching it. For even if the crime may perhaps be called Herod’s (Matthew 14:10), still he was of Israel’s blood. That is why Christ, charging the peoples of the Jews with their insolence against every holy man, says: ‘It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem’ (Luke 13:33).
Palladius: So the inspired Baptist too was a light and a lamp for those under the law in Judea, by likeness to Christ and by sharing in him.

Cyril: That is what I say. And in the same way we say that the holy apostles are to be understood as loaves. For only one is bread by nature and in truth: the bread that is from heaven and gives life (John 6:33). But by imitation of the one who is bread by nature, and by sharing in him, the divine guides into the mysteries are loaves that nourish us in godliness, putting into us words of life and driving the famine of ignorance out of the souls of those who believe. The loaves are equal in number to the disciples, for they are twelve, and they are laid in two rows, six on this side, it says, and six on that (Leviticus 24:6), almost as if they stood round in a circle, with the one Bread from heaven, that is, Christ, lying in the middle. And each is of two tenths (Leviticus 24:5), that is, of two perfect measures. For the inspired disciples became perfect in both respects, ready for every good thing, distinguished in deed and in word.
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §15 ends 'and the statement is true', and §16 continues with γάρ, so the English begins with an ellipsis under Cyril's label. 'The shadow in the law' cited to Hebrews 10:1 ('the law has a shadow of the good things to come'). Psalm 132:17 = LXX Psalm 131:17 ('I have prepared a lamp for my Christ'). John 5:35: Cyril's 'teachers of the Jews' (καθηγηταῖς) refers to those who sent to John (John 5:33). Paul and the lamp of the first tent: Cyril treats Hebrews as Paul's; Hebrews 9:2 names 'the first tent' with its lampstand and table, the very phrase Cyril uses, so 'all but calls to mind' (μονονουχί, since Hebrews names the lampstand, λυχνία, not the lamp) is cited to Hebrews 9:2 (reviewer; replaces an earlier flag that took 'Paul' as a possible slip). The John 5:35 words are Christ's; 'burning' echoes καύσουσιν in Leviticus 24:3. Herod: allusion to the beheading of John (Matthew 14:10; also Mark 6:27); Cyril's claim that Herod was 'of Israel's blood' is kept as he states it. Luke 13:33 quoted closely. John 6:33 for 'the bread from heaven that gives life' (compare John 6:51). 'Six on this side … and six on that' with 'it says' is Cyril's paraphrase of Leviticus 24:6 (two rows of six), not the LXX wording. 'Two perfect measures' renders δύο μέτρων τελείων, kept literal because it sets up the play on 'perfect' (τέλειοι). Uncited possible echoes: 'words of life' (John 6:68; Philippians 2:16), 'famine' (Amos 8:11), 'ready for every good thing' (πρὸς πᾶν … ἀρτίως ἔχοντες ἀγαθόν; 2 Timothy 3:17 or Titus 3:1, with a play on ἄρτος / ἀρτίως that English cannot carry), 'in deed and in word' (Luke 24:19). θεσπέσιος rendered 'inspired' throughout; χορός rendered 'company'. ἕνα τε καὶ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ: masculine ἕνα takes up 'the one bread by nature' (εἷς ... ἄρτος) of the previous sentence, so rendered 'the one Bread from heaven'. διά γε τὸ προσδραμεῖν rendered 'in that they ran': it states how their brief delight showed, not its cause.

title: Frankincense, salt and the Sabbath, and why these types stand in the first tent
english: Cyril: Frankincense and salt are sprinkled on the loaves (Leviticus 24:7). The frankincense points to the sweet fragrance of sanctification and to the fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:15); the salt hints at understanding. For the word of the saints is not senseless or foolish but, as it is written, seasoned with grace and salt (Colossians 4:6), and it gives grace to those who hear (Ephesians 4:29). Christ also said to them, ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13). The loaves are set out on the Sabbath day as well (Leviticus 24:8). For the day on which the holy apostles were made known is the time of the spiritual Sabbath, that is, the coming of Christ. Because those of Israel did not recognize it, Paul says of them, ‘So then there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God’ (Hebrews 4:9). For they did not enter into his rest, because they did not accept faith (Hebrews 3:18–19). The spiritual and true Sabbath rest, then, is the time when our Savior came to dwell among us. The loaves are set out before the eyes of God, and indeed before the eyes of Israel as well. For ‘you shall set them out,’ he says, ‘on the Sabbath day before the Lord continually, from the sons of Israel’ (Leviticus 24:8). They are before the eyes of God, because he looks on the saints and continually counts them worthy of his care; for ‘the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous,’ it says (Psalm 34:15). They are before the eyes of Israel, because Israel ought to give heed to them and, as it were, fixes on them the eye of the mind, of which the bodily eye would be a type. ‘But they shall belong,’ he says, ‘to Aaron and to his sons, and they shall eat them’ (Leviticus 24:9). For the writings of the holy apostles are set before us as food: before us who have been justified in faith, a holy and sacred race, peoples for his own possession (1 Peter 2:9), chosen and anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit.
Palladius: Well said; I would agree. But why are the types of the holy Baptist and of the holy apostles not in the Holy of Holies but in the first tent?

Cyril: First, because the distance between them is great, and what belongs to the saints will not be placed where Christ is, but, as it were, outside and in a lesser place. For the things of God are set apart and stand by themselves, and a wide distance walls off what is human, showing that the distinct character of the natures and the difference in glory admit no comparison. Second, because they came from the Jews and from the worship under the law. For this reason the first tent is, so to speak, the place fitting for them, the tent in which stood the altar of burnt offerings, one of the types. Or did the calling of the holy disciples not come from the blood of Israel and, as it were, from the first tent?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: Since our account of these things is now well and sufficiently settled, we should bring in, if you agree, the voice of the inspired Paul, which sets out clearly and elegantly the testimony concerning the first and the second tent. He writes as follows: ‘Now when these things had been prepared in this way,…’ (Hebrews 9:6)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-turn: Cyril's speech continues from §16 (no speaker mark in the source row), so it is labelled 'Cyril:'. Leviticus 24:7: the salt on the loaves comes from the Septuagint, which adds καὶ ἅλα to the frankincense; the Hebrew has frankincense only. Leviticus 24:8: the printed quotation reads παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ ('from the sons of Israel'), where the Septuagint has ἐνώπιον τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ ('before the sons of Israel'); Cyril's comment ('before the eyes of Israel') presupposes the Septuagint wording. The English follows the printed text in the quotation; a reviewer may prefer to restore 'before'. Psalm 34:15 = LXX Psalm 33:16 (also quoted in 1 Peter 3:12). 2 Corinthians 2:15 cited for 'fragrance of Christ' (Χριστοῦ εὐωδία); Ephesians 4:29 for 'gives grace to those who hear' (ἵνα δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσιν), combined with Colossians 4:6 under 'as it is written'. Hebrews 3:18–19 cited for 'they did not enter His rest ... because of unbelief'; Hebrews 4:6 is a close alternative. Uncited possible allusions: ἀνάδειξις ('public appearing') may echo Luke 1:80; 'justified in faith' (Romans 5:1) and 'anointed with the grace of the Spirit' (2 Corinthians 1:21; 1 John 2:20) are too general to cite. 'Peoples for His own possession': λαοῖς τοῖς εἰς περιποίησιν, plural, from 1 Peter 2:9; 'His' supplies the implied owner as the English Bible versions do. 'A wide difference': πολὺς λόγος here means a great measure or distance, not 'word'. The altar 'of burnt offerings' (τῶν καρπωμάτων) is placed by Cyril in the first tent; in Exodus 40:6, 29 that altar stands before the door of the tent. Translated as printed, no correction. Hebrews is quoted as Paul's, as Cyril holds. The Hebrews 9:6 quotation is cut at the column break (PG 68.681/684) and continues in §18. Reviewer: ἐφιστῶντος is parallel to ὀφείλοντος (Israel ought to attend and, as it were, fixes the mind's eye), not governed by 'ought'; ἀσύγκριτον governs both the distinct character of the natures and the difference in glory; Εἶτα ὅτι γεγόνασιν has the Baptist and the apostles together as subject ('they'). Lev 24:8 παρά kept as printed (see above).

title: Christ the high priest enters once for all with His own blood
english: Cyril: ‘…the priests continually go into the first tent, performing the services; but into the second the high priest goes alone, once a year, not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people. By this the Holy Spirit makes clear that the way into the holy places has not yet been disclosed while the first tent still has its standing. This is a figure for the present time, in which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the worshiper as to the conscience; they deal only with foods and drinks and various washings, ordinances of the flesh imposed until a time of reformation. But Christ, having come as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, entered once for all into the Holy of Holies, having obtained eternal redemption’ (Hebrews 9:6–12).

You understand, then, that the priests performed the services in the first tent but had no way of entry into the Holy of Holies. For such, in a way, is the worship under the law: it has its standing in shadows. And these things are of no use for cleansing and washing away sin. For you heard Paul just now cry out that they cannot perfect the worshiper as to the conscience (Hebrews 9:9). Rather, it was kept until the time of reformation (Hebrews 9:10), which plainly means the time when the Only-begotten became man, when what was unlovely in the types passed over into the truth. ‘Once a year the high priest alone used to enter the Holy of Holies, and not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people’ (Hebrews 9:7). The most wise Paul will make this plain to us again, speaking of Christ in these words: ‘When he said above, “Sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin you did not desire, nor did you take pleasure in them” (these are offered according to the law), “then I said, Behold, I have come to do your will.” He takes away the first in order to establish the second. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ.
