And every high priest stands day after day ministering and offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but he, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sat down for ever at the right hand of God, waiting from then on until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet. For by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are being sanctified’ (Hebrews 10:8–14). For having died once, he dies no more, as it is written (Romans 6:9–10); and having borne the sins of many (Hebrews 9:28), he entered into the Holy of Holies, that is, into heaven, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf (Hebrews 9:24).

Palladius: Your explanation is clear. So you may leave off your labor on that point. But tell me, since I ask: what blood, again, was the one who presides over the sacred rites accustomed to bring for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people?
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation: Paul's Hebrews 9:6–12 begun at the end of §17 continues across the column break (PG 68.684); labelled 'Cyril:' because the quotation is in his turn. Cyril's text of Hebrews 9:12 reads εἰς Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων ('into the Holy of Holies') where the New Testament has εἰς τὰ ἅγια; and Hebrews 9:9 has καθ' ὃν (referring to the time) where most New Testament texts read καθ' ἥν. Both translated as Cyril has them. The second 'Once a year...' (Hebrews 9:7) is Cyril's restatement in the past tense; it is in quotation marks in the print and cited. Hebrews 10:8–9 quotes Psalm 40:6–8 (LXX Psalm 39:7–9) and 10:13 echoes Psalm 110:1 (LXX 109:1); the citation is given to Hebrews, the passage Cyril quotes. Hebrews 10:11: Cyril's text reads ἀρχιερεύς ('every high priest'), a reading also found in part of the New Testament manuscript tradition; most printed texts have ἱερεύς ('every priest'). Translated 'high priest' as printed. Hebrews 10:12: the printed Greek (PG 68.684) reads οὐδεμίαν ('no sacrifice'), which reverses the verse; the English follows οὗτος δὲ μίαν ('but He, having offered one sacrifice'), the New Testament reading. An earlier lane reported that the Latin version printed beside it in PG 68.683 reads 'hic autem, cum unam pro peccatis hostiam obtulisset'; I did not re-check the Latin column myself. 'For ever' in 10:12 is placed with 'sat down'; the Greek εἰς τὸ διηνεκές can also go with 'offered one sacrifice for sins'. 'Having died once, He dies no more, as it is written' joins Romans 6:9 (οὐκέτι ἀποθνήσκει) and 6:10 (ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ). 'The types, which had no beauty of their own, gave way to the truth' renders τῶν τύπων τὸ ἀκαλλὲς μετακεχώρηκεν εἰς ἀλήθειαν (literally 'the unloveliness of the types changed over into truth'). Palladius' ἱδρῶτα ... μέθες ('let go the sweat on this') is taken as 'you may put down your labor on that point'. Reviewer: Hebrews 10:9 in Cyril's printed text reads τότε εἶπον ('then I said', the wording of Psalm 40:7, LXX 39:8) where the New Testament has τότε εἴρηκεν ('then he said'); translated as printed. The words 'He takes away the first in order to establish the second' (Hebrews 10:9b) stand outside the quotation marks in the print; they are verbatim Hebrews and kept inside the cited quotation. Palladius' τὸν τῶν ἱερῶν ἡγούμενον: ἱερῶν is the neuter 'sacred rites' (priests would be ἱερέων), so 'the one who presides over the sacred rites', not 'the chief of the priests'. πάλιν in Σαφηνιεῖ ... πάλιν restored as 'again'. The Hebrews 10:12 emendation (οὐδεμίαν → οὗτος δὲ μίαν) is accepted: the printed word contradicts the verse and Cyril's own next sentence; the Latin column was not re-checked in this review.

title: The law of the sin offering for the anointed priest and for the people
english: Cyril: Paul was learned in the law and had mastered the commandment given through Moses as thoroughly as anyone. So he speaks of things so holy and so far beyond words to the Hebrew people as to men wise in such matters, who had read the law: not in long accounts, but rather in passing, as a reminder of what they already knew. But if you agree, I will bring forward the law on this point as well, since you have chosen to learn what is profitable and are very thirsty for an exact and finely worked explanation of these insights. It is written, then, in Leviticus:

‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel: If a person sins unintentionally before the Lord against any of the commandments of the Lord concerning things that ought not to be done, and does any one of them; if the anointed high priest sins so as to make the people sin, he shall bring for the sin he has committed a calf from the herd, without blemish, to the Lord as a sin offering. And he shall bring the calf to the door of the tent of witness before the Lord, and he shall slaughter the calf before the Lord. And the anointed priest, whose hands have been consecrated, shall take some of the blood of the calf and bring it into the tent of witness. And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times before the Lord, in front of the holy veil. And the priest shall put some of the blood of the calf on the horns of the altar of the compounded incense, which is before the Lord, which is in the tent of witness; and all the blood of the calf he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offerings, which is by the doors of the tent of witness. And all the fat of the calf of the sin offering he shall remove from it: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is on the thighs, and the lobe on the liver together with the kidneys, he shall remove it, just as it is removed from the calf sacrificed as a peace offering; and the priest shall offer it up on the altar of burnt offering. As for the skin of the calf and all its flesh, with the head, the extremities, the belly and the dung, they shall carry the whole calf out of the camp to a clean place, where they pour out the ashes, and they shall burn it on wood with fire; it shall be burned on the place where the ashes are poured out’ (Leviticus 4:1–12).

This is what the law commanded to be done if any fault committed in ignorance should be charged against the one who holds first place in the priesthood. It says too that for the sins of ignorance of the people a sacrifice must be performed: a calf is brought and slaughtered in the same way at the doors of the tent of witness before the Lord, the elders of the congregation lay their hands on it, its blood is brought into the Holy of Holies, and, in a word, everything is done with it in the likeness of the sacrifice for Aaron (Leviticus 4:13–21). But that Christ is the cleansing of priests and people alike (for in him we have been justified, wiping away the stain that comes from sin)…
translator_notes: The long quotation is Leviticus 4:1–12 in the Septuagint; it matches the LXX closely, with small differences (Cyril has ἐναντίον for ἔναντι in 4:2 and ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν προσταγμάτων). 'The anointed priest' renders ὁ ἱερεὺς ὁ χριστός, the Septuagint's term for the high priest; it is not a title of Christ here and is not capitalized. 'Whose hands have been consecrated' renders ὁ τετελειωμένος τὰς χεῖρας (literally 'perfected as to the hands', the LXX idiom for priestly ordination). 'Peace offering' renders θυσία τοῦ σωτηρίου, the LXX term for the sacrifice of well-being. 'Thighs' renders μηρία; English Bibles from the Hebrew have 'loins'. 'The altar of burnt offering' at 4:10 renders θυσιαστήριον τῆς καρπώσεως. Cyril's summary of Leviticus 4:13–21 (the people's sin offering) says the blood is brought 'into the Holy of Holies'; Leviticus 4:16–18 has it brought into the tent of witness and sprinkled before the veil. Blood is taken inside the veil only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). Translated as printed, no correction. 'Elders of the congregation' renders οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τῆς Συναγωγῆς (Leviticus 4:15). The section ends mid-word at the column break (PG 68.685/688): ἀπο|τριβόμενοι μολυσμόν. The English in §19 already supplies 'wiping away the stain that comes from sin' so the clause reads whole; when merging with §20, its opening should begin from the main clause ('…these things too would make this plain to anyone') and not repeat 'wiping away the stain'. The opening parenthesis in the last sentence closes in §20. Reviewer: ψυχή in Leviticus 4:2 rendered 'a person' (Hebraism); περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας 'as a sin offering'; the anacoluthon in Leviticus 4:11–12 smoothed with 'As for' without changing the sense.

title: The unblemished calf and the blood sprinkled seven times
english: Cyril: …will be clear to anyone from these things too. But let us take up, one by one, what belongs to each point of the text; for so the discussion would go forward clearly and unfold, as far as it can, what is hidden.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: The calf, then, is taken without blemish and without wound (Leviticus 4:3) as a type of Christ, who is truly without blemish and did not submit to the wound that sin inflicts. ‘For the ruler of this world is coming,’ he says, ‘and he will find nothing in me’ (John 14:30); for he committed no sin, as the Scriptures say (1 Peter 2:22). And it is brought to the very doors of the holy tent, before the Lord (Leviticus 4:4); so Christ, as it were, did not refuse to suffer for the holy tent, that is, the Church, and was dedicated for her as a fragrant aroma to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2). That is why he said, ‘For their sake I sanctify myself’ (John 17:19). By ‘I sanctify’ he means ‘I bring and dedicate an unblemished offering to God the Father.’ For whatever is dedicated to God is said to be sanctified, as in the saying somewhere in Scripture: ‘It is a snare to a man to sanctify hastily something of his own, for after he has made the vow he comes to regret it’ (Proverbs 20:25). The words ‘before the Lord’ show that the offering is acceptable and well pleasing. For we already know what is written about the pair of brothers, I mean Cain and Abel: ‘God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts,’ it says, ‘but to Cain and his sacrifices he paid no heed’ (Genesis 4:4–5). For it is plain enough that God looks upon what pleases him, and turns away in hatred from what does not. When the hands of the one who has sinned have been laid on the calf, the slaughter is carried out, and that before the Lord (Leviticus 4:4). For ‘he takes away our sins and suffers pain for us’ (Isaiah 53:4) as he is slain; for the hand stands as a type of deeds and actions. Yet he is slain before the Lord, the Father all but consenting that the Son must die for us. For the Father does not turn away when he sees him slain; not that he in any way praises the suffering, but he knows well that Emmanuel’s suffering for us brings salvation to the world. So it is he who takes away our sins and suffers pain for us (Isaiah 53:4), enduring for our sake the slaughter on the precious cross. Then the priest takes some of the blood on his finger and sprinkles it seven times on the holy veil (Leviticus 4:6), which was over the ark, and whose name is the mercy seat. He also smears the horns of the altar of incense (Leviticus 4:7). For Christ has become for us both atonement (1 John 2:2) and mercy seat (Romans 3:25). Yet it is in the blood of an eternal covenant (Hebrews 13:20) that he grants us the most perfect cleansing. This, I think, is the meaning of the mercy seat being sprinkled seven times with the blood, for the number seven is a sign of perfection. For his death too is fragrant with the salvation and life of the world, and with our access to God in faith. ‘For one died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised’ (2 Corinthians 5:14–15), as the Scriptures say. So the smearing of the golden altar of incense with the blood shows the fragrance of his death. The rest of the blood is poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offerings (Leviticus 4:7)…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing Cyril's turn from section 19 ('But that Christ is the cleansing of priests and people alike, for we have been justified in him, ...'); the 'Cyril: …' label follows the Book 10 continuation convention. ἀπλήξ ('unstruck', 'without wound') is Cyril's own word beside ἄμωμος; Leviticus 4:3 has only ἄμωμος, so the citation marks the unblemished calf. John 14:30: Cyril reads εὑρήσει οὐδέν ('will find nothing') where the Gospel text has οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέν; translated as Cyril has it. 'He committed no sin' cited to 1 Peter 2:22 (exact wording; it echoes Isaiah 53:9). Ephesians 5:2 cited for ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας applied to Christ's self-offering. Proverbs 20:25 is the LXX text (same verse number in English Bibles, though the Hebrew sense differs). The clause 'ἐφορᾷ γὰρ ὅτι τὸ ἁνδάνον ... οὐκ ἀσυμφανές' has awkward word order in PG; read as 'that he looks upon what pleases him ... is not unclear', so the γάρ is left implicit. Isaiah 53:4 is LXX (οὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται); Cyril writes αἴρει ('takes away'), perhaps under John 1:29; rendered as he has it. The subject of the slaughter sentences shifts from the calf to Christ (masculine participles), so 'he' is used. Cyril identifies the 'holy veil' of Leviticus 4:6 (where the LXX has κατὰ τὸ καταπέτασμα, 'before the veil') with something over the ark called the mercy seat; translated as he states it, not harmonised. θυμιατήριον here means the golden altar of incense (as in Hebrews 9:4), not a hand censer. 'Access in faith' (προσαγωγή) may echo Romans 5:2 or Ephesians 3:12; left uncited as doubtful. The section ends mid-word (καρπω|μάτων); English closes the phrase 'altar of burnt offerings' here, and section 21 resumes with 'in the outer tent'.

title: The calf burned outside the camp; the tent anointed
english: Cyril: …in the outer tent. The blood stands as a type of life (Leviticus 17:11), and Emmanuel has laid down his life (John 10:15) not only for the Church from the Gentiles but also for those under the law, that is, for Israel. For all of us together, Greeks and Jews alike, have been redeemed by the blood of Christ, and Paul will bear witness, saying: ‘Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith’ (Romans 3:29–30). When the inner parts of the calf have been taken out and carried up to the altar (Leviticus 4:8–10), the rest of the body is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:11–12). For he himself is the holy sacrifice, fragrant with virtues, of which the inner parts would be types, since the virtues are hidden, as it were, within us and lie deep within the mind. He is also the one who suffers outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), and by the death of his own flesh cleanses those who were defiled. For ‘the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on those who are defiled,’ it says, ‘sanctify for the purification of the flesh’ (Hebrews 9:13). So Emmanuel, being one and the same, gives off his fragrance in the holy tents, I mean the churches, and he also suffered outside the gate; and there, as the inspired Paul said, we too must go out, bearing his reproach (Hebrews 13:13). A calf is also brought for the sins of ignorance of the people (Leviticus 4:13–14), in the same way and without any difference, and the meaning of the sacrifice was the same in every case. For Emmanuel offered himself in the same way for small and great, for people and priests alike. Or is what I say not true?
Palladius: How could it not be?
Cyril: Shall we, then, rein the discussion back, as it were, and turn again to the accounts of the tent?
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: When all the work had been completed, and each of the holy vessels had been carefully set in the place most fitting for it, God laid down that they and the tent must be sanctified, saying to the inspired Moses: ‘And you shall take the oil of anointing, and anoint the tent and everything in it, and you shall sanctify it and all its vessels, and they shall be holy. And you shall anoint the altar of burnt offerings and all its vessels, and you shall sanctify the altar, and the altar shall be holy of holies’ (Exodus 40:9–10). So you see the ark anointed with the holy oil, and the table too, and the lampstand beside it, and the golden altar of incense as well; and indeed our long discussion has already made clear that in all of them Emmanuel is portrayed.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: Consider, then, what is sung by the voice of David as addressed to him: ‘You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions’ (Psalm 45:7). Paul also writes: ‘For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one’ (Hebrews 2:11). We must understand that, by reasoning free from all fault, the very one who…
translator_notes: Opens mid-phrase: ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ σκηνῇ completes 'the altar of burnt offerings' from section 20. 'The first tent' (Hebrews 9:2, 6 language) is rendered 'the outer tent' for clarity. ψυχή is rendered 'life' twice ('a type of the life', 'laid down his life') to keep Cyril's link between the blood and Christ's self-giving; Leviticus 17:11 (ἡ ψυχὴ πάσης σαρκὸς αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐστιν) is cited as the evident basis for 'blood = soul/life'. 'Laid down his life' cited to John 10:15 (τὴν ψυχήν μου τίθημι). 'Redeemed by the blood of Christ' may echo 1 Peter 1:18-19 or Ephesians 1:7; left uncited as general. Hebrews is quoted as Paul's, as Cyril regards it. ἐντόσθια = the inner parts (fat, kidneys, liver lobe of Leviticus 4:8-10). Hebrews 13:13 is paraphrased without 'to him' (πρὸς αὐτόν), as Cyril has it. Exodus 40:9-10: verse numbers agree in LXX and English. ἅγιον ἁγίων is kept as 'holy of holies' (not 'most holy') because section 22 builds on the phrase, calling the law 'holy of holies' and Christ 'the Holy of Holies'. Psalm 45:7 = LXX Psalm 44:8 (LXX numbering converted). ἀδικία rendered 'lawlessness' following the usual English of this verse; literally 'injustice/wrongdoing'. The section ends mid-sentence ('αὐτὸς ὑπάρχων ὁ | τοῖς ἄλλοις ...'), continued in section 22.

title: Christ sanctified in his humanity; the cloud fills the tent
english: Cyril: …as God, together with God the Father, supplies and bestows sanctification on all others, is himself sanctified with us in his humanity; and this is what is called the self-emptying (Philippians 2:7). For he who is holy by nature, as God, is said to have needed God to sanctify him. Blessed Peter says this too: ‘Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit’ (Acts 10:38). So the anointing concerns his humanity, and the sanctification belongs to the flesh, which is not holy by nature but holy by participation in what comes from God. For sanctification comes to created things from outside, and they are enriched with grace as something added to them by God. Together with the rest, the altar of the worship under the law is anointed too. For the law also is holy: it calls its hearers to the knowledge of him who is God by nature, plants in them an understanding of righteousness, and carries those it instructs on to the beginnings of goodness. ‘For the beginning of a good way,’ it says, ‘is to do what is right’ (Proverbs 16:7, Septuagint). And the inspired Paul writes somewhere: ‘So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good’ (Romans 7:12). The law is holy of holies, not in its shadow, but because, if it is turned to spiritual contemplation, its types proclaim aloud to us Christ himself, who is truly the Holy of Holies. For as God he sanctifies those who have come to share in him through faith, anointing them with his own Spirit. Now that the holy tent has been set up, and anointed with the holy oil as well, let us speak of what comes next, if you agree.
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: This, then, is what is written: ‘And Moses finished all the works. And the cloud covered the tent of witness, and the tent was filled with the glory of the Lord. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of witness, because the cloud overshadowed it, and the tent was filled with the glory of the Lord. Whenever it went up from the tent, the sons of Israel set out with their baggage; but if the cloud did not go up, they did not set out until the day on which the cloud went up. For the cloud was on the tent by day, and fire was on it by night, before all Israel in all their journeys’ (Exodus 40:33–38). For when the holy and truer tent, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, had been revealed in the world, the light of Christ shone around it, and the cloud, like a kind of spiritual dew richly nourishing us with what comes from above, fills the divine temple. Yet Moses, it says, was not able to enter; for Israel did not go in, since it could not bear the force of the divine light. For it neither understood the mystery of Christ, nor accepted the enlightening that comes in the Spirit, nor beheld the glory of the Lord with the eyes of the mind. And with him, as in the type of the cloud, when he departs from the world and goes on to the things above, we depart too, following in the Master’s footsteps; for he opened for us the new and living way (Hebrews 10:20), I mean the way to the things above and in heaven. And when he rests, as it were…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing 'the very one who' from section 21. 'Self-emptying' (κένωσις) cited to Philippians 2:7 (ἐκένωσεν). Acts 10:38: PG prints Ἵνα, which cannot stand; the verse reads Ἰησοῦν τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρέθ, so 'Jesus' is read (probably a misread abbreviation of the name); flagged for the source editor. εἰσποιητῶς ('by way of addition/adoption') rendered 'as a gift brought in'. Proverbs 16:7 is the LXX verse (Brenton 16:7, 'The beginning of a good way is to do justly'); it has no counterpart at 16:7 in English Bibles, which follow the Hebrew; the editor may prefer '(Proverbs 16:7, Septuagint)' in the reading text. Holy of holies: neuter for the altar (section 21), masculine for the law (agreeing with νόμος) and for Christ (τὸν Ἅγιον ἁγίων), capitalised only for Christ. Exodus 40:33-38 cited by English numbering (Moses finishing the work is 40:33b; LXX verse division in this chapter differs slightly). The PG text of the quotation lacks 'the cloud' as subject of 'whenever it went up' (LXX has ἡ νεφέλη); translated 'it' as printed. σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου rendered 'tent of witness'. 'Eyes of the mind' may echo Ephesians 1:18 and 'beheld the glory of the Lord' 2 Corinthians 3:18; 'following in the Master's footsteps' may echo 1 Peter 2:21; all left uncited as doubtful. Hebrews 10:20: ἐνεκαίνισεν ... ὁδὸν πρόσφατον καὶ ζῶσαν, cited. The section ends mid-sentence ('ἀναπαυομένῳ δὲ ὥσπερ | καὶ καταλύοντι...'), continued in section 23.

title: Light in the Churches; sacrifice at the tent alone
english: Cyril: …and lodges, we rest with him and shall lodge with him. When the cloud set out, the people set out with it; and when it halted, they camped with it (Numbers 9:17–18). ‘For the cloud,’ it says, ‘was over the tent by day, and fire by night’ (Exodus 40:38). For Christ richly nourishes with spiritual gifts those who have come to be, as it were, in day and light, because they have grasped the knowledge of him with precision and careful study and have had their minds made bright; and he enlightens those who are still less instructed. But in the Churches there is no darkness of worldly deceit at all, since Christ shines all around them and floods all things with spiritual light; for we are not of night or of darkness, but sons of light and of day, as it is written (1 Thessalonians 5:5).
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: To this we shall add an account, and not at great length, of the laws concerning the tent, of the gifts the peoples brought, and also of the settings out and the encampments. For in this way our discussion would keep to a straight road.
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: The Lawgiver and Judge, then, ruled that sacrifices must be offered in the holy tent alone by any who chose to offer them. He was drawing them away, I suppose, from the stale false worship, that of Egypt, I mean, where there was much mockery of idols and a most unlovely crowd of falsely named gods, a crowd perhaps unknown even to those who had chosen to worship them; and where sacrifice was left free, to be offered as anyone pleased, just as one of the Greek sages carelessly said: ‘One man sacrificed to one god, another to another.’ Drawing them away, then, from so cold and profane a habit and so senseless a custom, he said again in Leviticus: ‘Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: This is the word which the Lord has commanded, saying: Any man of the sons of Israel, or of those who reside among you, who slaughters a calf or a sheep or a goat in the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness to make it a whole burnt offering or a peace offering to the Lord, acceptable as a fragrant odor; and whoever slaughters outside, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness, and so does not offer a gift to the Lord before the tent of the Lord, it shall be reckoned to that man that he has shed blood; that soul shall be utterly destroyed from its people’ (Leviticus 17:2–4). He says, then, that the one who sacrifices outside the tent sheds blood and will be liable to the charge of murder. For such a man has, as it were, killed himself and destroyed his own soul, since he withdraws it from him who is God by nature, assigns it to stones and wood, and dedicates it to the deceits of demons. That he did not command simply every slaughtered animal to be brought to the doors of the tent, but only whatever anyone chose to dedicate to God as a sacrifice, he showed clearly by adding at once (Leviticus 17:7): ‘And they shall not offer their sacrifices…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing Cyril's turn from section 22 (Christ, as in the type of the cloud, departs and we depart with him; when he rests, as it were, and lodges...); the 'Cyril: …' label follows the Book 10 continuation convention. καταπιαίνει ('fattens', 'enriches') echoes section 22's image of the cloud as spiritual dew; rendered 'richly nourishes'. Numbers 9:17-18 is cited for the cloud's setting out and halting (a clear allusion; the quotation itself is Exodus 40:38 LXX). 1 Thessalonians 5:5 is quoted loosely and reordered. The line 'ἄλλος δ' ἄλλῳ ἔρεζε θεῶν' is Homer, Iliad 2.400 (Cyril's 'one of the Greek sages'); not Scripture, so no inline citation. τῶν λαῶν δωροφορίας is plural ('the peoples'), probably the tribal gifts of Numbers 7; kept as 'the peoples' and not cited. Leviticus 17:2-4: Migne omits προσηλύτων in the first clause ('those who reside among you'); in the second clause Migne reads ἔξω ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν ... καὶ μὴ ἐνέγκῃ αὐτὸ, ὥστε μὴ προσενέγκῃ (LXX: ἔξω καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν ... μὴ ἐνέγκῃ αὐτὸ ὥστε προσενέγκαι); rendered 'and so does not offer', which keeps Migne's negative without changing the sense. σωτήριον = 'peace offering' (LXX 'offering of salvation'). The quotation of Leviticus 17:7 breaks across sections 23/24; Migne's ἐπὶ τὰς θυσίας is likely a misprint for LXX ἔτι τὰς θυσίας ('no longer'); 'no longer' is not added. 'Stones and wood' is a common biblical idiom for idols (compare Deuteronomy 4:28); left uncited as a general phrase. 'Deceits of demons' may echo Leviticus 17:7 / 1 Corinthians 10:20; uncited.

title: One house for the lamb; the Church and the heretics
english: Cyril: …to the vain things after which they themselves go whoring’ (Leviticus 17:7). So he altogether forbids sacrificing indiscriminately to whomever one wishes, and says, very rightly, that worship must be offered to him alone who is God by nature.
Palladius: Our argument stands very well indeed.

Cyril: I think it would also benefit us not a little to understand, in another way, that it is profitable, and indeed in some sense necessary, for the sacrifices to be performed and the sacred victims offered in the holy tent alone.
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: Did we not say that the calf slaughtered at the holy tent for the priest and for the people’s sins of ignorance is an image and type of Emmanuel (Leviticus 4:3, 13–14)?
Palladius: We did.

Cyril: In this way, then, we say, the mystery of Christ must be celebrated in the Churches of God, as in holy tents. For he sketched this out for us again elsewhere too. For when, at the beginning, he laid down for the Israelites departing from the land of the Egyptians how the lamb must be slaughtered as a type of Christ, he says: ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside’ (Exodus 12:46). So the heretics, who think otherwise, set aside what God has decided: beside the tent that is truly holy they pitch another for themselves; they sacrifice the lamb outside, carry it far away from the one house, and divide him who cannot be divided; for Christ is one and complete in all. But our wise Moses, who reveals holy things to us, gives this charge in Deuteronomy: ‘Take care that you do not offer your burnt offering in every place that you see, but only in the place which the Lord your God chooses, in one of your cities; there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I command you today. But you may slaughter whenever you desire, and eat meat as your soul desires, according to the blessing of the Lord your God which he has given you in every city. The unclean among you and the clean alike shall eat it, as they would a gazelle or a deer; only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water’ (Deuteronomy 12:13–16). To dare, then, to sacrifice in every place, and not to fulfill the mystery of Christ in the house of God, is the offense of a most loathsome mind, and liable to indictment.
Palladius: Well said. But explain this to me. The law has condemned the eating of blood, and very reasonably. What, again, might be the meaning contained in the letter?

Cyril: Then, if you agree, let us cite what was decreed on this point in Leviticus as well. It runs thus (Leviticus 17:10–14): ‘And any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes residing among you, who eats any blood, I will set my face against the soul that eats the blood, and I will destroy it from its people. For the soul of all flesh is its blood…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation, completing Leviticus 17:7 from section 23 (Migne ἐκπορνεύσωσιν; LXX ἐκπορνεύουσιν, same sense). Leviticus 4:3, 13-14 cited for the calf offered for the anointed priest's sin and for the people's sins of ignorance (ἀγνοήματα), which Cyril discussed earlier in this book; a clear allusion. Exodus 12:46 matches LXX in sense (LXX adds ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας). Deuteronomy 12:13-16: Migne reads 'in one of your cities' (πόλεων) where LXX 12:14 has 'tribes' (φυλῶν); followed Migne. Migne has singular τὸ ὁλοκαύτωμά σου in 12:13; kept singular. αὐτόν after ἐκλέξηται (Hebraism, 'chooses it') is absorbed into 'the place which the Lord your God chooses'. ἀλλ' ἢ ἐν πάσῃ ἐπιθυμίᾳ σου θύσεις rendered 'But you may slaughter whenever you desire'. κεκιβδήλευκεν (literally 'has marked as counterfeit') rendered 'has condemned'. ἱεροφάντης ('revealer of sacred rites') rendered 'who reveals holy things to us'. 'Dividing him who cannot be divided' may echo 1 Corinthians 1:13 and 'one and complete in all' may echo Colossians 3:11; both doubtful, left uncited. The section ends inside Leviticus 17:11 before ἐστι; the English places 'is' in natural order here and section 25 resumes with 'And I have given it'.

title: Blood as a type of the immortal soul; no leaven with the blood
english: Cyril: …And I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls; for its blood shall make atonement in place of the soul. Therefore I have said to the sons of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood, and the proselyte residing among you shall not eat blood. And any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes residing among you, who takes in hunting a beast or a bird that may be eaten, shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth. For the soul of all flesh is its blood. And I said to the sons of Israel: You shall not eat the blood of any flesh, for the soul of all flesh is its blood; everyone who eats it shall be utterly destroyed’ (Leviticus 17:10–14). See, then, how clearly and openly the blood is taken as a type of the soul.
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: The law, therefore, sets the blood apart and draws it away from the bodies of the slaughtered animals, teaching a true doctrine, one received by us in faith and held in honor in the Churches: I mean that the rational soul of man is immortal, and continues to exist and to think. Death does not destroy it together with earthly bodies; rather, the Creator releases it and sets it free, and exempts it from suffering, having made it a sharer in life. For in the beginning man was made a living soul, when God breathed into him the breath of life; for so it is written (Genesis 2:7). For, I think, we shall be charging the Life that gives life to all things with weakness if we say that what came into life from it perishes together with our temporary bodies. But we shall crown that Life with the most excellent wisdom if we believe that the soul is immortal, since the Creator of all, in whom we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28), has willed that it be so. And this, I suppose, is the reason for the legislation on this point. But let us go on to other ordinances of the tent as well. God said, then, in Exodus: ‘You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leaven’ (Exodus 23:18). Let the blood that is shed be unleavened, he says, the blood shed for what has been brought to God as a sacrifice; that is, of course, no leaven, or fine flour that has been leavened, is to be brought with it. For we must be cleansed and, as it were, unleavened, that is, we must not harbor in our minds any entanglement, so to speak, with baseness and wickedness, and so consecrate to God our own souls, of which the blood is a type. And the inspired Paul also called those ‘a new batch’ and ‘unleavened’ (1 Corinthians 5:7–8) who keep their own soul sincere, unclouded and unmixed with baseness, through faith in Christ, of course, and through perfect love. But ‘neither shall the fat of my feast,’ he says, ‘remain overnight until morning’ (Exodus 23:18); that is, you shall not offer yesterday’s fat as a fragrant odor. And in Leviticus he sets out the law more clearly and makes the matter plain, saying of the one who brings a sacrifice (Leviticus 7:16–17): ‘If he sacrifices his gift as a vow or a freewill offering, on whatever day he offers his sacrifice it shall be eaten, and on the next day as well; but what is left of the flesh of the sacrifice until the third day shall be burned with fire…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation (Leviticus 17:11, after ἐστι); the inline reference (Leviticus 17:10–14) covers the whole quotation begun in section 24, as does the citation placed at its start in section 24. ψυχή is kept as 'soul' throughout the quotation because Cyril's argument turns on it (blood as type of the soul's immortality). ἀντὶ ψυχῆς rendered literally, 'in place of the soul'. διακεῖσθαι καὶ φρονεῖν is compressed and difficult; taken as 'continues in being and in understanding' (that the soul survives death in a conscious state). In 'we shall crown it with the most excellent wisdom' the object of στέψομεν is unexpressed; taken as the Life of the previous sentence (we honor that Life as supremely wise), parallel to 'charging the Life with weakness'; doubtful. τῆς ... ζωογονούσης ζωῆς is God, hence 'Life' capitalized. Genesis 2:7 is paraphrased, not quoted. Exodus 23:18 LXX: Οὐ θύσεις ἐπὶ ζύμῃ αἷμα θυσιάσματός μου, οὐδὲ μὴ κοιμηθῇ στέαρ τῆς ἑορτῆς μου ἕως πρωί; both halves are cited at their clauses (compare the parallel Exodus 34:25, not cited). The phrase ὑπὲρ τοῦ προσκεκομισμένου is taken as 'the blood shed for what has been brought to God as a sacrifice'. 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 supplies νέον φύραμα, ἄζυμοι and εἰλικρίνεια. The Leviticus 7:16-18 quotation continues into section 26. Exodus 23:18: Cyril has σφάξεις ('slaughter', the verb of Exodus 34:25) where LXX 23:18 has θύσεις; rendered 'offer', the usual English for this verse, since 'slaughter the blood' is not English; the rest of both halves matches 23:18. Cyril's 'Let the blood ... be unleavened' is his own paraphrase with φησί, so it carries no quotation marks.

title: Leftover sacrifices and the end of the law in Christ
english: Cyril: …But if he does eat any of the flesh on the third day, it shall not be accepted for the one who offers it; it shall not be credited to him; it is a defilement; and the soul that eats of it shall be defiled and shall bear the sin’ (Leviticus 7:18). So the sacrifice of the third day is rejected; and that yesterday’s is refused as well, he made plain by saying: ‘If you sacrifice to the Lord a sacrifice, a vow of rejoicing, you shall sacrifice it so that it is acceptable for you. On that same day it shall be eaten; none of the flesh shall be left until morning; I am the Lord’ (Leviticus 22:29–30); ‘he shall bear the sin’ (Leviticus 19:8).
Palladius: Then what might be the meaning of these as well?

Cyril: The law has shown us many times already in what came before that divine Scripture is accustomed to divide the whole of time sometimes into two: the time when the law was in force, and the time when Christ shone forth; and sometimes again into three, inserting and placing between them the time when the choir of the holy prophets shone forth; except that in the time of Moses and in that of the holy prophets the manner of worship was the same, since it was still in the shadows of the law. But when morning has come, that is, when the third season has at last been revealed in turn, and the spiritual light, that is, Christ, shines all around the world beneath the sun, and the ancient mist has at last been dispersed, the manner of worship of that former time is no longer acceptable. Whether the fat or the sacrifice is yesterday’s or the third day’s, it is no longer acceptable, but loathsome and rejected before God, and counted as a defilement for those who choose to bring it out of season. Or would you not say it is true that, now that Christ illumines the souls of the saints with the teachings of the Gospel and initiates them so well into spiritual worship, the things in the law have somehow become superfluous and useless?

Palladius: I would. For I will call to mind the inspired Paul, who called the law’s grounds for boasting refuse and loss because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). And I hear him writing to some: ‘I tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing’ (Galatians 5:2).

Cyril: You are right. So it is sin and defilement, now that Christ has been revealed and the time of the law and the prophets has gone by, to cling to worship as in shadows, and to attempt to bring to God a sheep, or fat, or frankincense, even though the Son says plainly to God the Father: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said: See, I have come, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book, to do your will, O God’ (Hebrews 10:5–7; Psalm 40:6–8). For the Son, offering himself up for us as a spotless victim (Hebrews 9:14), put a stop to the things of the law, which could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:11); for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets (Romans 10:4).
Palladius: Well said.
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation, completing Leviticus 7:16-18 from section 25; Migne adds μιανθήσεται ('shall be defiled') to LXX 7:18, kept. The second quotation is Leviticus 22:29-30 LXX (εὐχὴν χαρμοσύνης, 'a vow of rejoicing'); its last clause, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν λήψεται, is not in 22:30 and matches Leviticus 19:8 (also 7:18), so it is cited separately; the old English's Leviticus 19:5-8 for the whole quotation was wrong. Προαποδέδειχεν ἡμῖν ὁ νόμος: Migne reads 'the law' (ὁ νόμος); with ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ('in what came before') it may be a misprint for ὁ λόγος ('our discussion'); translated as printed. καὶ τὰ τάττοντος μεταξὺ is corrupt in Migne; sense taken as a third period inserted between. The time-scheme: 'morning' stands for Christ's coming, the third period after the law and the prophets; any legal offering kept over, 'yesterday's' or 'the third day's', is no longer acceptable. Cyril's present tenses are kept. Galatians 5:2: Migne prints ἡμᾶς ('us'), an itacistic slip for NT ὑμᾶς; rendered 'you'. Philippians 3:7-8 supplies σκύβαλα, ζημία and τὸ ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως. The Son's words match Hebrews 10:5-7 verbatim (σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι, οὐκ ηὐδόκησας); LXX Psalm 39:7-9 = English Psalm 40:6-8 (renumbered). 'Spotless victim' alludes to Hebrews 9:14 (ἑαυτὸν προσήνεγκεν ἄμωμον); 'could not take away sins' reproduces Hebrews 10:11 (περιελεῖν ἁμαρτίας). Romans 10:4 has 'end of the law'; Cyril adds 'and the prophets'. The 'shadows' of the law echo Hebrews 10:1 and 'the time of the law and the prophets' echoes Luke 16:16 / Matthew 11:13; both general, left uncited.

title: The newborn offering and the eighth day
english: Cyril: So then, after the perfecting in Christ, the Father cannot be approached through the worship of the law; he can be approached through the Son alone. That is why he said, ‘No one comes to the Father except through me’ (John 14:6). And that everything not in Christ is unfit for sacrifice and imperfect, while what is through him and in him is acceptable and most holy, can also be seen clearly from what the law says. In Exodus it says, ‘You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk’ (Exodus 23:19); and in Leviticus, ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When a calf or a sheep or a goat is born, it shall be seven days under its mother; but from the eighth day on it shall be accepted as gifts, an offering by fire to the Lord. And a calf or a sheep, the mother and her young, you shall not slaughter on the same day’ (Leviticus 22:26–28). So he does not allow a lamb that is newborn and still at the breast to be slaughtered, showing that what is still immature and, so to speak, small and weak in understanding is not yet holy, and for this reason is still unacceptable to God. Such were certain unwise and small-minded people to whom the inspired Paul writes: ‘For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the first principles of the oracles of God; you have come to need milk, not solid food. But solid food belongs to the mature’ (Hebrews 5:12–14). What is still on milk and at the breast is therefore immature, I mean in understanding and in spiritual strength. But let our discussion of these matters now move, as from a type drawn from things that are seen and plain to the senses, to things beyond the senses and grasped by the mind; only, you will understand very well that in Christ all things have come to perfection and acceptance. For the animals that are brought and dedicated to God must, he says, be seven days under their mother, but from the eighth day on they will be a gift, and an offering by fire to God.
Palladius: Your point is not very clear.

Cyril: Do you not say that the eighth day is the day of the Savior’s resurrection, and the beginning, as it were, of a new age, once the time of the law, figured in the first seven days, has passed by?
Palladius: I do.

Cyril: Then whatever belongs, so to speak, to the time of the law, that is, whatever lies in worship according to the flesh, is still unholy and cannot yet be offered; but from now on everything in Christ, on the eighth day and after, is already a gift and well pleasing to God. For the calling in Christ has no end, and its beginning is the resurrection. The Son himself knew this, and so he said at one time, ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself’ (John 12:32), and at another, ‘Truly I tell you, unless the grain falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears more fruit’ (John 12:24).
Palladius: You have spoken rightly. But the rule that a mother must not be killed…
translator_notes: Exodus 23:19 is cited; the same LXX words recur at Exodus 34:26 (and Deuteronomy 14:21), so the reference could be either Exodus place. Cyril says the law 'does not allow the lamb to be slaughtered', blending the Exodus milk rule with the Leviticus seven-day rule; kept as he wrote it. κάρπωμα rendered 'offering by fire' (LXX term for a burnt portion). Leviticus 22:28 in Cyril's text reads 'calf and sheep, it and its young'; rendered 'calf or sheep, the mother and her young' for sense, since αὐτήν is feminine (the dam). John 12:24: Cyril has πλείονα ('more fruit') where John has πολύν ('much fruit'); followed Cyril. The eighth day as the resurrection day is Cyril's reading, not a Scripture citation; the 'new age' idea carries no citation. The section ends mid-sentence in Palladius' question; it continues in section 28.

title: The mother spared with her young; no grove beside the altar
english: Palladius: …together with her young on the same day: what, in turn, would that mean?

Cyril: After laying down in the law so well what concerns Christ, and gracefully foretelling the perfecting that comes through him, the Lawgiver, being God, did not fail to know the disobedience of the Jews and the unruliness of Jerusalem. He knew that for this reason the people of Israel would be destroyed as killers of the Lord and as men who had savagely abused the Son; yet Jerusalem would not perish altogether, root and all. She would remain like a woman bereft of children, waiting for the last time, at the end, when she too will be saved, running behind the nations. For she has been set at the back, that is, behind, as the Psalmist’s words have it: ‘For he will put them at the back’ (Psalm 21:12). For all Israel will be saved, once the flock from the nations has first been gathered into the divine folds (Romans 11:25–26). So the law does not allow the destruction to come about as a final and total ruin. It shows in advance that the wrath against the disobedient is tempered with gentleness; and at the same time, I think, it sets the matter before us as a kind of figure of something we need to know. For the things that exist will by no means pass away into nothing, overpowered by unchecked corruption. Rather, they will endure, as it were, through succession, this one preserved in that, and that perhaps in this, according to kinship or likeness of kind, since God wards off the total destruction of his own creatures. For ‘he created all things that they might exist, and the generations of the world bring preservation’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:14), as it is written. And it was fitting that the foretelling of such things, and indeed their disclosure, should belong to the teaching about Christ, for whose sake and in whom what was corrupted is saved, and what was under the tyranny of death has blossomed again into life. For the root of the human race died like a mother, as in Adam (1 Corinthians 15:22); yet those who came from it, that is, we ourselves, have blossomed again in Christ. In him we exist and are saved, since we have him as our life and as a second root, so to speak, of our race.
Palladius: How well, and how carefully, your argument is worked out!

Cyril: It is worth adding to what has been said, Palladius, this passage: ‘You shall not plant a grove for yourself; any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God you shall not make for yourself; you shall not set up a pillar for yourself, things which the Lord your God hates’ (Deuteronomy 16:21–22). See how he removes the worshipper of the truth entirely from idolatrous deceit. He by no means allows him to make use of the laws of the pagans, and he charges him to shake off their customs, even if they do no harm and even if they come about by chance.
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: The pagans would take over the most flourishing trees and every thicket dense with leaves, and there they would set up altars and sacrifices to the demons. For they had to, they simply had to, attach to the altars of the demons something that would carry the mind away, as it were, and worldly pleasures besides. Falsehood is sick with weakness from within, but it is often decked out with ornaments brought in from outside,
translator_notes: Opening line completes Palladius' question begun at the end of section 27 (Leviticus 22:28). Psalm 21:12 is English numbering; LXX Psalm 20:13 reads ὅτι θήσεις αὐτοὺς νῶτον ('you will make them turn their back'); Cyril's text has third person θήσει and he reads νῶτον as 'behind', so rendered 'he will put them at the back' to keep his argument. 'All Israel will be saved' quotes Romans 11:26; the flock from the nations entering first alludes to Romans 11:25, hence 11:25–26. Wisdom of Solomon 1:14: σωτήριοι means 'wholesome' or 'bringing preservation'; rendered 'bring preservation' because Cyril's argument (kinds preserved through succession) rests on that sense. 'As in Adam' taken as a clear allusion to 1 Corinthians 15:22. The subject of 'having legislated' is not named in the Greek; 'the Lawgiver, being God' supplies it from ὡς Θεός. τύπων ὥσπερ τινὰ ... εἰδήσεως ἀναγκαίας is awkward (τύπων may be a misprint for τύπον); rendered 'a kind of figure of something we need to know'. ἀπεζεσμένως taken in Cyril's usual sense 'carefully, with refinement'. Ἕλληνες rendered 'the pagans' (Cyril means pagan worshippers, not Greeks as a nation). Deuteronomy 16:21: Cyril's text reads οὐ ποιήσεις σεαυτῷ where the common LXX text has ὃ ποιήσεις σεαυτῷ ('the altar ... which you will make for yourself'); followed Cyril. The section ends mid-sentence; it continues in section 29. δι' ὃν (accusative) rendered 'for whose sake', not 'through whom'.

title: No pagan adornment for God’s altar; the leaders’ gifts begin
english: Cyril: …as, of course, shameless women are too. But what need did the divine altar, flashing with the beauty of the truth, have of help from outside, that is, of needless ornaments? For the divine is not approached through worldly pleasure, nor with a mind that is somehow slack and fastened on the things of the flesh, but with an understanding that is sober and looks intently upward, to the heavens. If a divine altar had happened to stand somewhere, perhaps even at the foot of trees, as if by chance, the thing would have done no harm at all to the steadfast and genuine worshipper of the Savior. But since the practice is wholly pagan, we must refuse to imitate it, and refuse any likeness to the custom. In the same way, of course, for the faithful mind, firmly set on true knowledge, an idol is nothing in the world (1 Corinthians 8:4), and neither is food offered to idols anything (1 Corinthians 10:19); yet such a person is not permitted to eat when another warns him, for the sake of the conscience of the weaker (1 Corinthians 10:28). ‘For why am I judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanks, why am I denounced over that for which I give thanks?’ (1 Corinthians 10:29–30). So this wins approval with God: I mean refusing to act as the pagans do, both in the placing of altars and in the customs and ways of worship.
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: Sacred Scripture again made it plain to us that we must bear fruit for the glory of God and not go into the holy tent with empty hands. In Numbers it runs thus: ‘And it came to pass on the day that Moses finished setting up the tent, that he anointed it and sanctified it, and all its furnishings, and the altar and all its furnishings; he anointed them and sanctified them. And the leaders of Israel brought offerings, twelve leaders of their fathers’ houses. These were the leaders of the tribes; these were the ones who oversaw the census. And they brought their gift before the Lord: six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon from every two leaders and a calf from each, and they brought them before the tent. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take them from them, and they shall be used for the work of service at the tent of witness, and you shall give them to the Levites, to each according to his service. And Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites’ (Numbers 7:1–6). The tribal leaders’ gifts did not stop there; others were brought besides. For it is written: ‘And the leaders brought offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day he anointed it, and the leaders brought their gifts before the altar. And the Lord said to Moses: One leader each day, a leader each day, shall bring their gifts for the dedication of the altar. And the one who brought his gift on the first day was Nahshon son of Amminadab, leader of the tribe of Judah. And he brought his gift: one silver dish weighing a hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels by the holy shekel,
translator_notes: Opening clause completes Cyril's sentence from section 28 (falsehood dressed up like shameless women). 'An idol is nothing in the world' quotes 1 Corinthians 8:4; 'nor is food offered to idols anything' follows 1 Corinthians 10:19; 'when another warns him' follows 1 Corinthians 10:28 (παρεγγυῶντος ἑτέρου; παρεγγυάω 'urge, charge', so the other person is warning against eating). The general theme of the weaker brother's conscience is also 1 Corinthians 8:7–13, left uncited to avoid doubling. 1 Corinthians 10:29: Cyril's text reads 'why am I judged by another conscience' (ἐγὼ κρίνομαι) where the received text has 'why is my liberty judged'; followed Cyril. χάριτι rendered 'with thanks' as in the verse; βλασφημοῦμαι 'spoken against'. Numbers 7:3: LXX μόσχον rendered 'calf', as in sections 30-34, where Cyril reads the calf as Christ. ἐπισκοπή in Numbers 7:2 is the census of Numbers 1, hence 'who had charge of the census'. Weights in Numbers 7:13 are in shekels; Cyril's text has '130 its weight' without the unit for the dish, which English fills from the following 'shekels'. The Numbers quotation runs on into section 30 (Numbers 7:13–17). ὡς ἐκ ταὐτομάτου rendered 'as if by chance' (not 'of itself', which could suggest a miracle).

title: The leaders’ daily gifts as a figure of Christ’s offering
english: Cyril: …both full of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; one incense dish of ten gold shekels, full of incense; one calf from the herd, one ram, one yearling lamb for a whole burnt offering; and one male goat for sin; and for a sacrifice of salvation two heifers, five rams, five male goats, five yearling ewe lambs. This was the gift of Nahshon son of Amminadab’ (Numbers 7:13–17). And they brought their gifts in turn, one after another, up to the twelfth, in the same way and with unvarying generosity, each being assigned the day appointed for him in particular (Numbers 7:18–83); for this was how God ordained it.
Palladius: And what then is the meaning of so varied an offering?

Cyril: The thing is an offering of fruit, Palladius; but woven into it, I think, is also a mystical meaning, which refers the riddle to Emmanuel and to ourselves. I will explain it again as well as I can. Now that the holy and true tent (Hebrews 8:2), that is, the Church, has been revealed in this world, Christ, shining out in it in many ways, is offered, one might almost say, by us and on our behalf, as a sacred victim to God the Father, a ransom and exchange for the life of all, the One who is worth as much as all. For since the Only-begotten became man as one of us, he offered himself to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2), as a kind of first offering and firstfruits of human nature, fragrant with holiness: a holiness that is his by nature and in essence, inasmuch as he is understood to be God and is God, but that is his in turn as something received, because of his humanity. And though he is one, he was depicted in many ways, as in the offering of the leaders; and so too, even now, Christ is offered in sacrifice through those who serve as leaders in each age, being understood in many ways and honored with various names. The offering each day suggests, in a way, that the sacrifice of Christ never fails and never ceases on any day, and that those who have been justified by faith bear fruit in it. For worshippers will not fail, nor will there be any lack of gifts. Christ will be offered by us and on our behalf, mystically sacrificed in the holy tents. He himself is our first and choicest offering of fruit; for he offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father, not for himself, indeed, as irreproachable reasoning holds, but rather for us who were under the yoke and indictment of sin. And in likeness to him we too are sacred victims, dying to the world, since sin has been put to death in us, and living to God (Romans 6:11) the life of holiness and godliness. This, it seems, is what the leaders’ offering hints at for us. Would you like us to examine it part by part with fitting reasoning, as best suits us, and speak of it as far as we are able?
Palladius: By all means.
Cyril: Now a calf was brought by each leader, and the wagons, six in number, were assigned to the sacred work of the holy tent (Numbers 7:3–5). Then from…
translator_notes: Opening completes the Numbers 7:13–17 quotation begun in section 29. θυΐσκη δέκα χρυσῶν rendered 'incense dish of ten gold shekels' (LXX 'of ten [shekels] of gold'). θυσία σωτηρίου kept as 'sacrifice of salvation' (LXX for the peace offering) because Cyril reads it typologically later. δαμάλεις: LXX 'heifers' where the Hebrew has oxen; followed the Greek. Numbers 7:18–83 cited for the summary of the other eleven leaders' gifts. 'The holy and true tent' taken as a clear echo of Hebrews 8:2 (τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς). 'He offered himself to God the Father ... fragrant' cited to Ephesians 5:2 (offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma). Uncited possible allusions: 'ransom' (Mark 10:45; Matthew 20:28); 'exchange' (Matthew 16:26); 'firstfruits' (1 Corinthians 15:20); 'offered himself ... without blemish' (Hebrews 9:14), since Cyril's ἀμωμήτως modifies 'account', not Christ; 'sacred victims' (Romans 12:1). εἰσκεκριμένως: holiness is Christ's by nature as God, but 'received' or 'brought in' as man; rendered 'as something received, because of his humanity' to keep the contrast without overstating. 'Those who serve as leaders in each age' (οἱ κατὰ καιροὺς ἡγούμενοι) echoes the leaders of Israel and means the Church's bishops and priests; 'the holy tents' means the churches. ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ ὁσιότητι rendered 'of holiness and godliness'. Final sentence: 'a calf from each' and the six wagons assigned to the tent work refer back to Numbers 7:3–5; it breaks off mid-sentence and continues in section 31. ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν read as 'so too, even now' (then in figure, now in fact), not 'so to speak'. κατὰ τὸν ἀμωμήτως ἔχοντα λόγον rendered 'as irreproachable reasoning holds'.

title: Whole burnt offering and sacrifice of salvation; the dish and cup as Christ our food and drink
english: Cyril: …each, one silver dish and one cup, both, it says, full of fine flour mixed with oil; one incense dish full of incense; one ram and one yearling lamb for a whole burnt offering; a male goat for sin (Numbers 7:13–16). These are the whole burnt offerings. And for a sacrifice of salvation, it says, they also brought two heifers, five rams, five he-goats and five yearling ewe lambs (Numbers 7:17).
Palladius: Explain, then, before anything else, what separates the two: what difference would one say there is between the sacrifice of salvation and the whole burnt offering?

Cyril: Listen, then. In the whole burnt offerings the animals were burned up entire by the sacred and unquenchable fire, no part at all held back; every portion and every limb rose, as it were, to God as a fragrant aroma. But the animals slaughtered for the sacrifice of salvation received a partial consecration, in the right shoulder, for example, the head and the feet, the kidneys and the liver, and certain other inner parts and entrails. It is fitting, then, that Christ should be offered as a whole burnt offering, for he is truly holy in his entirety, wholly fragrant and sacred. But to us belongs what is not altogether holy and not entirely sacred, for there is some defilement in us too, because of the sin that is in us. For ‘no one is clean from filth’ (Job 14:4), and ‘Who will understand his transgressions?’ (Psalm 19:12), as it is written. For this reason the law very rightly commanded that the sacrifice of salvation be consecrated not as a whole burnt offering, but rather in part. Is the account clear to you, then, Palladius, and enough to make it easy to grasp?
Palladius: Very much so.
Cyril: Come, then, let us go on to the next point: to say something, I mean, about each of the things offered, and also to understand what is needed for our benefit.
Palladius: Go on, then.

Cyril: The gifts from each of the tribal leaders, then, are one silver dish and one cup, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. The dish serves for food and is useful for eating what goes with bread, as the Savior himself showed when he told John, his true disciple, who was eager to learn it, who would betray him: ‘He who dipped his hand in the dish with me,’ he says (Matthew 26:23). And why should I speak of the use of the cup, when the thing itself cries it aloud? Fine flour is a sign of bread, since bread is made from it, and the bread of life is Christ (John 6:35). So in the dish and the cup, as it were, and in the bread that was in both (for both were full of fine flour), as in food and drink, Christ is signified as life and as the giver of life. ‘For truly,’ he says, ‘I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves’ (John 6:53). And it says that the fine flour was soaked in oil, as though the type were singing out that very word in the Psalms (Psalm 45:7): ‘You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence; §30 ends 'Then from' (Εἶτα παρ'), so 'each brought' supplies the verb. The quotation is from the leaders' gifts in Numbers 7 (each day's list, e.g. 7:13–17); Cyril's list here leaves out the young bull (μόσχος) of 7:15, though he treats the calf in §32. LXX Numbers 7:17 has 'two heifers' (δαμάλεις) and 'ewe lambs' (ἀμνάδας) where the Hebrew has oxen and male lambs; 'heifers' is kept because Cyril's exegesis in §§32–34 depends on the female. θυσία σωτηρίου is the LXX term for the peace offering; rendered 'sacrifice of salvation' because Cyril builds on 'salvation' (see §34). θυΐσκη (LXX; RSV 'golden dish' for incense) rendered 'incense dish'. The partial consecration list (right shoulder, head, feet, kidneys, liver, inner parts) is Cyril's own summary and does not match any single verse (compare Leviticus 3:3–4; 7:32), so no citation. 'Unquenchable fire' recalls Leviticus 6:13 but is left uncited. Job 14:4 LXX reads 'Who will be clean from filth? Not one'; Cyril paraphrases. Psalm 19:12 = LXX Psalm 18:13. The dish saying matches Matthew 26:23 word for word (compare Mark 14:20), but Cyril sets it in John's question (John 13:23–26); cited to Matthew. PG φιλοπνευστοῦντι is read as φιλοπευστοῦντι ('eager to inquire'); a doubtful reading. ὀψοφαγία ('eating relish, cooked food with bread') rendered 'eating what goes with bread'. Psalm 45:7 = LXX Psalm 44:8; the quotation runs on into §32, and the citation is placed beside 'in the Psalms' here and at the close of the quotation in §32.

title: The incense dish, the four victims, and the heifers as ourselves
english: Cyril: …of gladness beyond your companions’ (Psalm 45:7). The incense dish, again, has the shape and form of a censer, being made like a small bowl, and it too is filled with incense. For Christ is both fragrance and censer. He does not have his fragrance from outside, as we ourselves do, who come to have it by sharing in virtue and in the holiness that belongs to godliness. He has it from within, as God, and is rich in his own nature in all for which he is wondered at, and he fills the whole world with a fragrance that is above the world and above creation. For since he is God by nature and in truth, and has in his own nature the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father (2 Corinthians 2:14), he is very clearly recognized for what he is. The incense dish, then, is full of incense. Accordingly there are brought a calf and a ram, and a lamb as well, and a male goat, the offerings brought in addition to these; and through them all he himself is portrayed. In the calf, because of its great strength, and because among the tame and clean animals the calf is foremost, and greatest in size of body; and all that is Christ’s stands in a spiritual pre-eminence, and he himself is the One who excels and stands above, by a difference beyond comparison in every respect whatever. In the ram, because of its full maturity; and in the lamb, because of its innocence: ‘For I,’ he says, ‘like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know’ (Jeremiah 11:19). In the male goat, because of the slaughter on behalf of those who had sinned. For under the law the male goat is the sacrifice for sin; and Emmanuel went down into death for our sake, and we have been redeemed from our ancient offences through the slaughter he endured for us. Or do you say that this too is not true?
Palladius: How could it not be?

Cyril: Notice, too, that the calves were brought, but were given for the work of the tent, so that when the camp moved they might carry the loads on wagons and spare those who performed the sacred service toil and distress (Numbers 7:3–8). For the Church rests upon Christ, and he carries us. He does not let the holy and precious race, the people skilled in holy works, fall into labours beyond their strength. In this way, then, the things named must be referred to Christ. As for the animals for the sacrifice of salvation, the leaders brought them, as it were, in place of themselves, consecrating them in some way to the holy tent and offering them up to God as a fragrant aroma. There were two heifers, five rams, five he-goats and five ewe lambs. Now the calf is Christ, and the heifers are we ourselves, and the reasoning about the two is not out of keeping, but rather true and plain. For the male is always, in a way, the one most fitted to lead, and held in the highest honour and glory with God; and nature is witness to it, admitting the fact. The female is lesser and placed beneath, coming as it were behind the strength and glory of the male. So in the male calf Christ is our leader, while we, as it were, are yoked beneath him and far less than he in strength and glory, and the distance between is beyond comparison. For even if he became like us…
translator_notes: Psalm 45:7 = LXX Psalm 44:8 (quotation begun in §31). θυΐσκη / θυΐα: Cyril explains the incense dish as censer-shaped, 'made like a θυΐα' (a small bowl or mortar); rendered 'made like a small bowl', a doubtful sense. ὁ γραφόμενος ('the one written/depicted') rendered 'portrayed'. 'Fragrance of the knowledge' echoes 2 Corinthians 2:14 (τὴν ὀσμὴν τῆς γνώσεως αὐτοῦ). Jeremiah 11:19 matches the LXX. 'Under the law the male goat is the sacrifice for sin' is a general reference (compare Leviticus 4:23; Numbers 7:16) and is left uncited. The calves given for the work of the tent refer to Numbers 7:3–8, where the leaders' twelve oxen and six wagons go to the Levites; Cyril calls the animals μόσχοι (calves), and ἱερουργοί ('sacred ministers', the Levites) is rendered 'the ministers'. 'Beyond their strength' (ὑπὲρ δύναμιν) may echo 1 Corinthians 10:13 and 'holy and precious race' may echo 1 Peter 2:9; both too loose to cite. The passage on male and female is translated as it stands. The sentence breaks off at 'For even if He became like us', continued in §§33–34.

title: The heifer is of one kind with the calf
english: Cyril: …(for the heifer is of the same kind as the calf), yet all that is his stands in a very great…
translator_notes: A one-line fragment between two PG column breaks (68.712–713). It completes the clause begun at the end of §32 ('For even if He became like us') and runs into §34 ('pre-eminence'). The English parenthesis reflects the explanatory γάρ clause; 'yet all that is His stands' takes τὰ αὐτοῦ from §34 so the split falls naturally.

title: Christ above us though made flesh; the two peoples and the flock of believers; our souls consecrated to God
english: Cyril: …pre-eminence. ‘For who will be likened to God among the sons of God?’ (Psalm 89:6). For Christ is at once like us and above us, in the pre-eminence of his Godhead, even though he became flesh (John 1:14). There are two heifers, as a type, I think, of the two peoples, who have run together into the one people made from both, as he who is for our sake and with us joins them through faith into spiritual unity (Ephesians 2:14–15). The rams, again, and the lambs, equal in number, and the male goats no fewer, point to the multitude of believers, the multitude gathered, I mean, in the fifth age, as it were, the time when he came who says, ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself’ (John 12:32). Through the rams is signified the believers’ maturity in understanding and their full growth in spiritual stature, the stature, plainly, that is in Christ (Ephesians 4:13); through the lambs, their simplicity and innocence: ‘Brothers,’ he says, ‘do not be children in your thinking, but be infants in evil, and in your thinking be mature’ (1 Corinthians 14:20); and through the male goats for sin, their constant need of cleansing and of the forgiveness of offences. That is why we too have been taught to say in our prayers, ‘Forgive us our trespasses’ (Matthew 6:12). For there is no time when those who are truly right-minded, and who know the weakness of human nature, need not cry out, ‘Who will understand his transgressions?’ and, ‘Cleanse me from my secret faults’ (Psalm 19:12). This is a spiritual sacrifice, giving off a fragrance to God for the salvation of our souls.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: I have said, then, that Christ is signified in the calf and in the rams, the lambs and the he-goats, and in the rest; and I would by no means suppose that the account given of this misses what is fitting. But if anyone should choose to carry the force of these thoughts over to ourselves as well, there is no harm in applying some such contemplation as this to the passage before us.
Palladius: What kind do you mean?

Cyril: Under the law the sacred victims were brought by all Israel, and the blood of the slain was poured out at the divine altar. The rite all but spelled it out, as in a shadow, and hinted to us indirectly that it is fitting for us to consecrate our own souls to the holy God.
Palladius: Well said.
Cyril: So the victims stand in our place and on our behalf, and in them it is we who, in type, are offered in sacrifice.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: Come, then, let us examine carefully, as is right, what was brought by the hand of the leaders as though from all the people, and look closely at the beauty of the spiritual contemplation. What was offered in silver vessels, I mean the dish and the cup, was fine flour soaked in oil. And the symbol of brightness…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing §§32–33. Psalm 89:6 = LXX Psalm 88:7, where the LXX reads 'to the Lord' (τῷ κυρίῳ); Cyril has 'to God' (τῷ Θεῷ). 'Even though He became flesh' alludes to John 1:14. The two peoples run together into one alludes to Ephesians 2:14–15 (τὰ ἀμφότερα ἕν, εἰς ἕνα καινὸν ἄνθρωπον); cited as an allusion. 'He who is for our sake and with us' may echo Emmanuel, 'God with us' (Matthew 1:23); left uncited. 'The fifth time' is Cyril's scheme of the ages, in which the fifth is the time of Christ's coming (compare Book 3); the fivefold rams, goats and lambs are read by it. 'Spiritual stature in Christ' alludes to Ephesians 4:13 (μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ). 1 Corinthians 14:20 is quoted with Cyril's word order. 'Forgive us our trespasses': Matthew 6:12 has ὀφειλήματα ('debts'); Cyril's παραπτώματα ('trespasses') is the word of Matthew 6:14; cited to the prayer in Matthew 6:12. Psalm 19:12 = LXX Psalm 18:13 (both clauses). 'For the salvation of our souls' plays on 'sacrifice of salvation' (θυσία σωτηρίου). The blood poured at the altar describes the rite generally (compare Leviticus 1:5; 3:2), and the link between blood and soul may rest on Leviticus 17:11, but Cyril quotes neither; no citation. θεωρία rendered 'contemplation' as elsewhere in Books 9–10. The section ends mid-sentence ('And the symbol of brightness…'), continued in §35 ('…is the silver').

title: The leaders’ gifts as types: gladness in hope, the one yoke of Christ, and meekness
english: Cyril: …is the silver; the fine flour is a symbol of life, since bread, which keeps us in life, is made from it; and the oil is a symbol of gladness. So let us too, for our part, offer to God who is over all, through our hope in Christ, the gladness that belongs to a bright life. For it says: ‘Rejoicing in hope’ (Romans 12:12). And how could those who keep the commandments of our Savior, and have trained themselves thoroughly in a life and conduct of shining distinction, not be filled with the highest joy? For them a share in his glory is stored up with God, wholly and surely. For it says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory’ (Colossians 3:3–4). So the fine flour is mixed with oil (Numbers 7:13). For in the life of the saints there is also the gladness that comes from the hope of glory, together, of course, with the brightness that belongs to holiness and righteousness. And the golden dish full of incense (Numbers 7:14) depicts the beauty of the saints: their fragrance in sanctification, held as in choice vessels, and then, as it were, a gift to God that is truly most fragrant. Or should we not think, Palladius, that the saints are bright and choice vessels?
Palladius: Certainly we should.

Cyril: Each leader also gave an ox, twelve in all. They carry the holy tent as their load, brought in pairs to a single wagon and under a single yoke, and they were assigned to the service of the Levites (Numbers 7:3–6). This would be a type of the two peoples, no longer divided by unlike doctrines and ways of life, but brought together and, as it were, running together under the one yoke of the Savior (Matthew 11:29), with endurance and courage. For it says: ‘Be courageous, and let your heart be strong, and wait for the Lord’ (Psalm 27:14). And the ox is an animal that endures hardship and is very strong. Such, surely, are those who have chosen godliness: they carry Christ upon themselves like a yoke, as the one prefigured in the holy tent. The divine Paul, too, called the Church his body (Colossians 1:24). And it was said to Ananias about him, I mean about Paul: ‘Go, for this man is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles’ (Acts 9:15). Besides these, a ram and a lamb were offered (Numbers 7:15). They hint at the coming to God of the older people and of the new, and at their dedication, so to speak, which is plainly a spiritual one. For just as endurance and courage were signified in the oxen, so in the same way, I think, the sheep clearly show the fruit borne in meekness by those who have been justified through faith in Christ. For the animal is gentle, and fruitful as well. Such are all who labor with exactness at the Gospel way of life, to whom Christ himself said: ‘Give to everyone who asks you, and from the one who takes what is yours do not demand it back; and to the one who strikes you on the cheek, turn the other also’ (Luke 6:30; Matthew 5:39). And Paul too writes: ‘The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §34 ends ‘Σύμβολον δὲ λαμπρότητος μὲν’ (‘and a symbol of brightness’), so the English begins ‘…is the silver’ under Cyril’s label, following the convention of other Book 10 chunks. The silver dish and bowl were named in §34 (Numbers 7:13); the citation is placed here at the flour mixed with oil. θυΐσκη (Numbers 7:14 LXX) rendered ‘golden dish full of incense’ (NETS ‘censer’; English Bibles ‘dish’ or ‘pan’). σκηνή rendered ‘holy tent’, the term most Book 10 chunks and Book 3 use. μόσχος παρ’ ἑκάστου, δώδεκα: these are the twelve oxen drawing the six wagons, one ox from each leader, two leaders to a wagon (Numbers 7:3), given to the Levites for their service (Numbers 7:5–6); μόσχος rendered ‘ox’ because the animals pull wagons; Cyril then treats them as the calf of the offering list. Psalm 27:14 = LXX Psalm 26:14. ‘The one yoke of the Savior’ cited to Matthew 11:29 (‘take my yoke upon you’) as a clear allusion. ‘Paul called the Church his body’ cited to Colossians 1:24 (‘his body, which is the Church’); Ephesians 1:22–23 says the same. The quotation of Acts 9:15 is exact apart from word order. TEXTUAL FLAG: ‘τοῦ τε πρεσβυτέρου προσενηνεγμένου καὶ τοῦ νέου λαοῦ’ has a stray participle ‘offered’ attached to ‘the older’; the sense is clearly ‘of the older people and of the new’, and Pass B translates that sense; ram = older people (Israel), lamb = new people (from the Gentiles), parallel to the two peoples under one yoke. Luke 6:30; Matthew 5:39 (reviewer): the first two clauses are Luke 6:30 (παντὶ αἰτοῦντί σε δίδου, ἀπὸ τοῦ αἴροντος τὰ σὰ μὴ ἀπαίτει); the cheek clause ends with Matthew 5:39’s ‘στρέψον αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην’ (Luke 6:29 has ‘πάρεχε καὶ τὴν ἄλλην’), so the quotation blends the two and both are cited. The quotation of 2 Timothy 2:24–25 begins at the end of this section and finishes in §36, where the citation stands. Uncited: ‘choice vessels’ for the saints (cf. 2 Timothy 2:21; Acts 9:15 follows) and ‘fragrance’ (cf. 2 Corinthians 2:15) are too loose for a citation.

title: The goat of confession, and the voice from above the mercy seat
english: Cyril: …toward all, teaching with meekness those who oppose him’ (2 Timothy 2:24–25). That the offering of a goat must follow what has already been named (Numbers 7:16) would show, I think, nothing other than what I said just now: that all people, even any whose settled character is good, need cleansing through repentance and the pardon of their trespasses. Knowing this, the divine David said: ‘If you should mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will stand?’ (Psalm 130:3). Under the old law, then, the goat was the sacrifice for forgiveness. But now repentance and the plea for pardon are the sacrifice for us who draw near to God in spirit and in truth (John 4:23). For it says: ‘State your sins first, that you may be justified’ (Isaiah 43:26). And David too sings somewhere: ‘I said, I will confess my sin against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart’ (Psalm 32:5). Is the account of the leaders’ gifts clear to you now?
Palladius: Entirely so.

Cyril: I think this too must be said. For when the sacrifice had already been brought by each, and as it were on behalf of all, the divine words began to come to Moses, the revealer of the sacred rites, in the holy tent. It is written thus, again in Numbers: ‘This is the dedication of the altar, after his hands were filled and after he was anointed.
