When Moses went into the tent of testimony to speak with him, he heard the voice of the Lord God speaking to him from above the mercy seat, which is on the ark of the testimony, between the two cherubim; and he spoke to him’ (Numbers 7:88–89). For when the holy tent had, as it were, been completed, and the true sanctuary, which is the Church, had been shown to the world, then indeed the voice of God the Father came to us. ‘For he has spoken to us in the Son’ (Hebrews 1:2), whom we also call the mercy seat for our sins, according to the Scriptures (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). The voice comes from above the cherubim, for God is above all creation and beyond it, and his supremacy over everything that has come into being belongs to his very essence and is inherent in him. And the Son, the true mercy seat, conveying to us the words that come from above and from the Father, said: ‘The words that I speak are not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 14:10, 24). So the voice came from above the mercy seat. You would also marvel not a little as you consider the approach of the tribal leaders. For a day was assigned to each one separately (Numbers 7:11), on which he was to carry out what had been prescribed and bring his gift. They came forward in good order, as the lawgiver decided; yet not in the order of their birth, that is, by age, nor simply mixed together at random, but arranged instead, as it were, in a mystical order.
Palladius: And yet I cannot work out what you mean. So tell me plainly.
Cyril: Would you like us to name, in order and one after another, those born of…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation, completing 2 Timothy 2:24–25 begun at the end of §35. Cyril’s text skips ‘apt to teach, patient’ (διδακτικόν, ἀνεξίκακον) between 2:24 and 2:25; the gap is his, not the translator’s. The goat ‘for sin’ is Numbers 7:16; Cyril uses both αἴξ and χίμαρος for it. Psalm 130:3 = LXX Psalm 129:3 (‘ἐὰν ἀνομίας παρατηρήσῃς, κύριε, κύριε, τίς ὑποστήσεται’). Isaiah 43:26 LXX (‘λέγε σὺ τὰς ἀνομίας σου πρῶτος, ἵνα δικαιωθῇς’), which the Hebrew-based English Bibles render differently; Cyril has ἁμαρτίας for ἀνομίας. Psalm 32:5 = LXX Psalm 31:5; Cyril has ἁμαρτίαν where the LXX has ἀνομίαν in the second clause. ‘In spirit and in truth’ cited to John 4:23 because it is the Gospel phrase that names the whole work. Numbers 7:88–89: the quotation starts at the last clause of 7:88 (‘This is the dedication of the altar…’) and runs through 7:89; LXX ‘μετὰ τὸ πληρῶσαι τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ καὶ μετὰ τὸ χρῖσαι αὐτόν’ is ambiguous (the masculine pronouns do not agree with the neuter θυσιαστήριον; Hebrew has ‘after it was anointed’), so Pass B keeps ‘his hands… he was anointed’ as the Greek stands. ἱεροφάντης rendered ‘who revealed the sacred rites’ to avoid the pagan term ‘hierophant’. ἱλαστήριον rendered ‘mercy seat’ throughout so the type stays visible; ‘the mercy seat for our sins, according to the Scriptures’ cited to Romans 3:25 (Christ as ἱλαστήριον) and 1 John 2:2 (‘for our sins’). John 14:24: Cyril’s wording blends John 14:24 (‘the word you hear is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me’) with John 14:10 (‘the words that I speak to you’); cf. John 7:16; (reviewer) the opening ‘τὰ ῥήματα ἃ ἐγὼ λαλῶ’ is John 14:10 and the close ‘τοῦ πέμψαντός με’ is John 14:24, so both are cited. ‘A day was assigned to each’ cited to Numbers 7:11 (‘one leader each day’). ‘The lawgiver’ (νομοθέτης) may mean God or Moses; left as Cyril has it. ‘Οἰκονομίαν μυστικήν’ rendered ‘a mystical order’. Section ends mid-sentence; §37 begins with ‘Ἰακὼβ’, so the English ends ‘those born of…’ and §37 opens ‘…Jacob?’

title: Not by birth order: Judah first, and the last made first
english: Cyril: …Jacob? For in this way the departure from that order in their approach would become very clear.
Palladius: By all means.

Cyril: Reuben, then, is the firstborn, and after him come Simeon, Levi and Judah, all from their mother Leah (Genesis 29:32–35). Bilhah, the servant girl, bore Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:4–8), and Zilpah, Leah’s maid, bore Gad and Asher (Genesis 30:9–13); and Leah, besides her other four, bore Issachar and Zebulun (Genesis 30:17–20). From Rachel, too, came Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 30:22–24; 35:16–18). So the first are the four from Leah, the free woman: Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah. From the two servant women, Bilhah and Zilpah, come four: Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. After these come another four: two from Leah, Issachar and Zebulun, and from Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin. We must also remember that Joseph’s lot was divided into two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, his sons (Genesis 48:5).
Palladius: I understand the order of the names very well. But it is now for you to make plain what, in all this, we are looking for.

Cyril: When they came forward with their gifts, Palladius, they did not come by age. First came Judah, though he was fourth in time (Numbers 7:12–17); after him Issachar, the ninth son, and with them Zebulun, the tenth (Numbers 7:18–29). After these came a second company, as it were: Reuben the firstborn, and Simeon, the next and second son (Numbers 7:30–41). Dan, a slave woman’s son, was joined to them as well. Next came a third rank, made up of three freeborn sons: Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin (Numbers 7:48–65). The fourth company, at the very end, is made up of those born of the servant women. These again are three, Dan, Asher and Naphtali (Numbers 7:66–83), although in the time of their birth they come before those placed ahead of them in order, I mean Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin. Would you not say this calls for close examination?
Palladius: Very much so. Try to tell me, then, what the reason is.

Cyril: The matter is a riddle, I think, once again. It shows that what comes through Christ holds the first rank with God over what belongs to the law, and that the first have been made last and the last first (Matthew 19:30). For those older in time, and for that reason firstborn, that is, Israel, come behind the Gentiles. And those who have the spirit of slavery (Romans 8:15), the sons of the Jerusalem that is in slavery, will yield the first place in glory to the sons of the free woman, who is the mother of us who have been justified in Christ (Galatians 4:25–26) and called to the dignity of the free through the Spirit of freedom. Look, if you will, at how exact these insights are. The tribe of Judah brings its gift first (Numbers 7:12), the tribe from which Christ sprang according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14). Right after it come Issachar and Zebulun, both free and born of free parents. Then Reuben, the firstborn…
translator_notes: Opens mid-question: §36 ends ‘τοὺς ἐξ’ and §37 begins ‘Ἰακὼβ γεγονότας;’, so the English opens ‘…Jacob?’. Birth order as Cyril gives it matches Genesis: Reuben 1, Simeon 2, Levi 3, Judah 4 (Leah, Genesis 29:32–35); Dan 5, Naphtali 6 (Bilhah, Genesis 30:4–8); Gad 7, Asher 8 (Zilpah, Genesis 30:9–13); Issachar 9, Zebulun 10 (Leah, Genesis 30:17–20); Joseph 11 (Genesis 30:22–24) and Benjamin 12 (Genesis 35:16–18) from Rachel. Joseph’s two tribes: Genesis 48:5 (also Joshua 14:4). Order of the gifts in Numbers 7: Judah day 1 (7:12), Issachar 2 (7:18), Zebulun 3 (7:24), Reuben 4 (7:30), Simeon 5 (7:36), Gad 6 (7:42), Ephraim 7 (7:48), Manasseh 8 (7:54), Benjamin 9 (7:60), Dan 10 (7:66), Asher 11 (7:72), Naphtali 12 (7:78). TEXTUAL FLAG: in the second company the Greek reads ‘Συνῆπται δὲ καὶ ὁ Δὰν ἐκ δούλης’ (‘Dan, a slave woman’s son, was joined to them’), but Numbers 7:42 has Gad on the sixth day, Dan appears again in the fourth company in this same section, and §38 names Gad (‘Συμεών τε καὶ Γὰδ, ὅς ἐστιν ἐκ δούλης’). Δάν is a slip, Cyril’s or a copyist’s, for Γάδ. Pass B translates the Greek as it stands; the editor may wish to print ‘Gad’ with a note. For that reason the second company is cited Numbers 7:30–41 only (Reuben and Simeon), and Gad’s day 7:42–47 is not cited here. ‘The first have been made last and the last first’ cited to Matthew 19:30 (‘many who are first will be last, and the last first’), whose order matches; Matthew 20:16 and Mark 10:31 are parallels. ‘The spirit of slavery’ cited to Romans 8:15 (πνεῦμα δουλείας). ‘The Jerusalem that is in slavery… the free woman, who is the mother of us’ is Galatians 4:25–26 (‘she is in slavery with her children… the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother’). δι’ ἐλευθέρου πνεύματος rendered ‘through the Spirit of freedom’ with a capital (cf. 2 Corinthians 3:17, uncited), since it answers the Spirit of adoption of Romans 8:15; a lower-case ‘a spirit of freedom’ is possible, and the reading is doubtful, so no citation. ‘From which Christ sprang according to the flesh’ cited to Hebrews 7:14 (‘our Lord sprang from Judah’); cf. Romans 9:5 for ‘according to the flesh’. The section ends in the middle of the word πρωτότοκος (‘πρω-’ / ‘-τότοκος’); the whole word ‘firstborn’ is placed here, so §38 should open ‘…Simeon and Gad’.

title: Reuben, Simeon and Gad stand for Israel, which comes after the free
english: Cyril: …and Simeon and Gad, who was born of a slave woman. Through these Israel is signified. Come, let us set out what belongs to each, gathering it from the prophecy Jacob spoke over them. The inspired Jacob said: ‘Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my children, hard to bear, hard and self-willed’ (Genesis 49:3). And again: ‘Simeon and Levi, brothers, carried out wrongdoing of their own choosing. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my heart not lean upon their gathering; for in their anger they killed men, and in their passion they hamstrung a bull. Cursed be their anger, for it was self-willed, and their wrath, for it was hardened’ (Genesis 49:5–7). And of Gad he said this: ‘A band of raiders shall raid, and he himself shall raid him at his heels’ (Genesis 49:19). So in Reuben Israel may fittingly be signified: firstborn in time, but hard, self-willed and insolent. In Simeon, with whom Levi is joined, Israel is signified as ready for bloodshed, as one who killed the saints (for ‘Which of the prophets,’ it says, ‘did your fathers not kill?’ (Acts 7:52)), and as one who hamstrung, so to speak, the bull, who is Christ. For it is not the Jewish people alone that stands convicted of daring these outrages against the saints and against Christ; Levi too joined them, that is, the priestly race, those who attend the altar, the scribes and Pharisees. That is why, in the prophecies of the forefather Jacob, Levi is yoked with Simeon. In Gad, who was born of a slave woman and is a band of raiders, Israel is signified as base-born in disposition, as testing Jesus and laying snares to do him harm; for they came to him saying, ‘Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?’ (Luke 20:22; Matthew 22:17). So, to bring my argument back to where it began: Israel, firstborn in time, hard, self-willed and insolent, quick to shed blood, whose wrath is cursed, who killed men and hamstrung the bull, base-born and bitter in deceit, who sets snares and is a band of raiders, has been ranked behind those who are in Christ and free; and even if it is free, it comes after us, so that it scarcely comes into the sight of God.
Palladius: You have put it well.

Cyril: You would understand what I mean more fully if you also turned your mind to what follows. For next, three in a row brought their offerings, descendants of Rachel the free woman: Ephraim and Manasseh [lacuna]. Then, after them, three more in a row, the sons of the maidservants: once again I mean Dan, Asher and Naphtali. Do you see, then, that the sons of the free woman go in first and are held in high honour, while the sons of the maidservants follow? Or is this not plainly what the inspired Paul himself writes to us? ‘When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,’ he says, ‘then all Israel will be saved’ (Romans 11:25–26).
translator_notes: Section opens mid-word (πρω|τότοκος) continuing the last sentence of §37 ('Then Reuben the firstborn'); the ellipsis marks the column break. Genesis 49 quotations follow the LXX (Hebrew differs, especially 49:6 'my glory' and 49:19 'raiders shall raid him, but he shall raid at their heels'). Gen 49:6 LXX μὴ ἐρεῖσαι τὰ ἥπατά μου, literally 'let my liver not lean/press', rendered 'let my heart not lean upon their gathering'. Gen 49:19: Cyril's text reads πειρατεύσει αὐτόν where LXX has αὐτῶν; πειρατήριον ('raiding band', also suggestive of 'trial/temptation') sets up his play with πειράζων ('testing Jesus'); the pun cannot be kept in English and is noted here only. Acts 7:52: Cyril reads ἀπέκτειναν ('kill') for the NT's ἐδίωξαν ('persecute'), probably blending Matthew 23:31/Luke 11:47; translated as he quotes it. The tribute question uses φόρους, closest to Luke 20:22 (φόρον); Matthew 22:17 has κῆνσον; both cited; the 'testing' recalls Matthew 22:18 (uncited, folded into the same episode). 'Those who attend the altar' echoes 1 Corinthians 9:13 (παρεδρεύοντες) only loosely; uncited. Closing clause καὶ εἰ ἐλεύθερος μεθ' ἡμᾶς, ὡς ἐν ὄψει μόλις ἔρχεσθαι Θεοῦ is elliptical; rendered 'even if it is free, it comes after us, scarcely coming into the sight of God'. Lacuna/defect: Cyril announces 'three' from Rachel but the print names only Ephraim and Manasseh and marks an asterisk; per §37 and Numbers 2:18-22 the third is Benjamin. Not supplied in the reading text. Romans 11:25-26: Cyril reads ὅταν ... τότε for ἄχρις οὗ ... καὶ οὕτως; translated as quoted. Reviewer: the print's asterisk after Manasseh marks the missing third name; per SOP 'preserve lacunae' the reading text now shows [lacuna] there rather than supplying Benjamin.

title: The camp set around the tent in the same order as the gifts
english: Palladius: You are right; the observation is very subtle indeed.

Cyril: And you will see very easily that this is no false conclusion. For Scripture at once bears us out from other points as well. God prescribed that the sons of Israel must break camp, and also halt, that is, encamp together, in fitting order, and he expressly commanded them to go around the tent, in keeping, I think, with what the blessed David sings so gracefully: ‘And I will go around your altar, O Lord, that I may hear the voice of your praise’ (Psalm 26:6–7), or again: ‘I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of joyful shouting’ (Psalm 27:6). But what they were commanded to do as in a type hints at something else as well. For we must not keep ourselves apart from God, but be seen, so to speak, standing near and all around him, with no sin coming between, no worldly pleasure setting us apart, while an upright steadiness of mind and a readiness for every admirable thing gather us into spiritual unity. For those who have chosen to win approval in this way, it is above all fitting that they bear fruit. For it is written: ‘All who are around him shall bring gifts’ (Psalm 76:11). So he commanded them to set out together with the tent and to march around it, and again in an order: not one that matched their ages and kept strict sequence from the first to the last, but with them joined together as they were, group by group, just as in the bringing of the gifts.

It is written thus in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Each man keeping to his own division, by their standards, according to their ancestral houses, let the sons of Israel encamp before the Lord; around the tent of witness the sons of Israel shall encamp’ (Numbers 2:1–2). Then he shows the place assigned to each, where and how they encamped, and who they were. For he goes on thus: ‘And those who encamp first, toward the east, are the division of the camp of Judah with their host; and those encamping next to them, the tribe of Issachar; and those encamping next, the tribe of Zebulun’ (Numbers 2:3–7). Then he mentions a second company and says: ‘The division of the camp of Reuben toward the south with their host; and the leader of the sons of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur; his host, those counted, numbered forty-six thousand five hundred. And those encamping next to him, the tribe of Simeon; and those encamping next to him, the tribe of Gad’ (Numbers 2:10–14). And at once he adds a third, saying: ‘The division of the camp of Ephraim by the sea with their host; and those encamping next, the tribe of Benjamin’ (Numbers 2:18–22). And then at once he mentions a fourth company, saying: ‘The division of the camp of Dan toward the north with their host; and those encamping next to him, the tribe of Asher; and those encamping next to him, the tribe of Naphtali. All those numbered,’ he says, ‘of the camp of Dan were one hundred fifty-seven thousand six hundred; they shall set out last…
translator_notes: LXX Psalm numbering converted: LXX Ps 25:6-7 = English Psalm 26:6-7 ('I will go around your altar, O Lord, that I may hear the voice of praise'; Cyril adds σου, 'your praise'); LXX Ps 26:6 = English Psalm 27:6 (LXX 'a sacrifice of praise and shouting'; Cyril omits 'praise and'; Hebrew lacks 'I went around'); LXX Ps 75:12 = English Psalm 76:11. Numbers 2 is quoted selectively: 2:1-2; Judah, Issachar, Zebulun 2:3, 5, 7; Reuben with leader and census 2:10-11, Simeon 2:12, Gad 2:14; Ephraim 2:18 and Benjamin 2:22 (Cyril skips Manasseh, 2:20); Dan 2:25, Asher 2:27, Naphtali 2:29, total and 'last' 2:31. The Dan quotation runs over into §40, so its citation is placed at the quotation's close there; it is listed here too. Cyril has πρὸς νότον where LXX Numbers 2:10 reads πρὸς λίβα; both mean the south side. 'By the sea' (παρὰ θάλασσαν) is the LXX idiom for the west side; kept literal. LXX names Ἐλισουρ υἱὸς Σεδιουρ given in the usual English forms Elizur son of Shedeur. Pass B splits the long Cyril turn into two paragraphs at 'It is written thus in Numbers'; the second paragraph continues the same Cyril turn and so has no new speaker label. ἐτύπου ('typified/ordained') rendered 'ordained' since the clause is about God's command; the type sense is picked up by Cyril himself in the next sentence (ὡς ἐν τύπῳ). ὁ λόγος rendered 'Scripture' (the account in Numbers).

title: Judah leads in the light; the maidservants’ sons set out last
english: Cyril: …by their divisions’ (Numbers 2:25–31). Do you see that Judah and those with him are placed first, and hold the chosen place toward the dawn and the south? For those who are in Christ are in the light, and fervent in the Spirit (Romans 12:11). Second comes Reuben and those with him. Third, again, are the sons of the free woman. Then after them come three others, the sons of the maidservants, of whom it is said, ‘They shall set out last’ (Numbers 2:31). Is it not plain, and in no way open to doubt, that the second, that is, the people in Christ, has been honoured above the firstborn and called in ahead of it, and so have those who are free in faith above those who come from slavery? For the one group leads because of Christ, who is from Judah; the others only barely follow behind, and have been placed, as it were, in the second rank.
Palladius: You have spoken most rightly, and I would praise you for such fine sharpness of mind.
translator_notes: Opens by closing the Numbers 2:25-31 quotation begun at the end of §39 (LXX 2:31 κατὰ τάγμα αὐτῶν; Cyril has the plural τάγματα). 'Toward the dawn and the south': Judah camped on the east (Numbers 2:3); Reuben, not Judah, held the south (2:10). Cyril appears to pair east/dawn with 'light' and south (νότος, the warm wind) with 'fervent', which explains the double phrase; translated as written. τῷ πνεύματι ζέοντες is a verbal echo of Romans 12:11 and is cited; 'in the light' may echo 1 John 1:7 or Ephesians 5:8 but is too general to cite. 'Christ, who is from Judah' recalls Hebrews 7:14 (ἐξ Ἰούδα); left uncited as a commonplace of the argument already made in §37. τοῦ πρωτοτόκου τὸ δεύτερον: 'the second [has been honoured above] the firstborn', with the genitive of comparison governed by προ- in both perfects; τῶν ἐκ δουλείας τὸ ἐλεύθερον ἐν πίστει rendered with plural persons for natural English. The old English row for §40 carried an extra closing doxology ('To God be the glory...') that is not in this source block; nothing was added here.
